1.3.title: BELOW EVERY THRESHOLD
1.3.situation: Over eleven weeks a customer makes cash withdrawals of €200, €150, €300, €200 and €250 from ATMs in three cities, buys a €180 prepaid card, and pays €340 for a short-term vehicle hire. Total activity: €1,620. No single transaction approaches any reporting threshold. The account is otherwise ordinary and funded entirely by salary.
1.3.question: What would a conventional AML monitoring system make of this?
1.3.answer: Almost certainly nothing. Every amount is unremarkable, the funding is clean, there is no structuring in the AML sense because nothing is near a threshold to be structured beneath, and the total over eleven weeks is consistent with ordinary living expenses. A system tuned for laundering has no rule that fires here. What is present, if you are looking for it, is a pattern rather than a transaction: cash extraction across multiple locations, conversion into an anonymous stored-value instrument, and a vehicle hire — a sequence that means nothing individually and something specific in combination. Whether that combination is worth acting on is Module 4's subject, and the honest answer is that on this evidence alone it is not. But no threshold anywhere would have raised the question. 19 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Most attacks in Europe over two decades cost under a few thousand euros; many cost under a few hundred. — Madrid 2004 is estimated at around €10,000; 11 September 2001, the outlier, at four to five hundred thousand dollars. — Threshold monitoring assumes criminal value is proportionate to criminal harm. In TF that assumption fails completely. — Lowering thresholds does not help — it multiplies alerts and still misses the four-hundred-euro transfer. — A financier moving small sums is not structuring; the amount is simply what was needed. — There is no de minimis. Two hundred and two million deserve the same treatment where the indicators are present. — The transaction carries almost no information. The case is in the counterparty, the pattern and what is known from elsewhere. 20

1.4.title: THE ALERT THAT NEVER FIRED
1.4.situation: After an attack, a review of the perpetrator's banking finds: eight months of ordinary salaried activity; three personal loans from three institutions in six weeks totalling €9,000, none repaid; a €4,000 cash withdrawal; and a series of small transfers to two individuals abroad. No monitoring alert was generated at any point by any of the three banks.
1.4.question: Was that a control failure?
1.4.answer: Partly, and the distinction matters. The small transfers and the salaried activity would not have alerted anywhere, and no reasonable system would have made them. The €4,000 withdrawal is unremarkable in isolation. But three unsecured loans from three institutions inside six weeks, none repaid, is one of the few genuinely detectable lawful-source patterns in terrorist financing — and it is invisible to each bank individually while being obvious across the three. That is not a tuning failure; it is a structural one, and it is why credit bureau data and information-sharing arrangements between institutions matter more in CFT than in most of compliance. The honest post-incident finding is that each institution's monitoring worked as designed, and the design could not see the case. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — AML monitoring assumes unexplained sources, layering, material value and deviation from pattern. All four fail in TF. — A system that passes a TF case may be functioning exactly as specified — this is a design limit, not a defect. — AML genuinely helps where the organisation funds itself through crime, since those proceeds behave like laundered money. — CDD, sanctions screening and the reporting infrastructure are shared, and screening is the most productive CFT control an institution has. — Identity replaces value, and pattern replaces threshold. — Context is decisive and mostly external — the institution supplies a fragment to somebody holding the rest. — Multiple unrepaid loans across institutions is detectable in aggregate and invisible to each bank alone. 22 MODULE 2 The international framework Counter-terrorist financing obligations come from a small number of instruments, and knowing which one you are acting under changes what you must do. This module covers the FATF recommendations that deal specifically with terrorist financing, the two United Nations designation regimes and why they work differently, what freezing without delay actually requires, and the recommendation on non-profit organisations — which has caused more harm through over-application than through neglect.

4.2.title: FOUR WEAK REASONS
4.2.situation: An escalation reads: 'Customer sends monthly transfers of €200–€400 to two individuals in a high-risk jurisdiction. Customer is from that jurisdiction. Transfers are frequent and small. The corridor is assessed as high risk for terrorist financing. Escalated for review.'
4.2.question: What has this escalation established?
4.2.answer: Nothing, and it is worth being precise about why. All four statements are true and all four are the same statement: this customer sends remittances home. Nationality, corridor, frequency and amount are not four independent observations — they are one demographic fact described four times, and the escalation reads as substantial only because it lists things. Nothing here distinguishes this customer from the several million people doing exactly this today. What would make it an escalation is a fact of a different kind: a recipient appearing on a designation, an unexplained funding source, a sequence involving cash conversion, or an answer to a question that does not hold up. The correct disposition on this evidence is no escalation and a recorded rationale saying so — and an institution whose escalation volume is made of files like this one has a discrimination problem and an intelligence problem at the same time, which is Chapter 4.4. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A designation match is not an indicator — it is a fact, and it is the strongest thing available. — Multiple unrepaid credit facilities is the rare strong signal on lawful-source financing, and needs cross-institution data to see. — Cash out then conversion to stored value is meaningful as a sequence and meaningless element by element. — Asking the customer is a control: a refused or changing explanation is one of the few indicators you can generate. — Weak indicators combine only where they are genuinely independent kinds of fact. — Corridor, community, frequency and small amounts are one demographic observation stated four times. — Establishing nothing is a legitimate outcome, recorded as such. 50

4.3.title: THREE CUSTOMERS, ONE RECIPIENT
4.3.situation: Three customers with no declared relationship each transfer between €300 and €500 monthly to the same named individual in the same country. The three live in different cities, bank at different branches, and have unrelated occupations. Their transfers fall in the same week each month.
4.3.question: Is this a network finding?
4.3.answer: It is a genuine one, and it is worth understanding what makes it different from the escalation in Chapter 4.2. The common recipient is a single fact that all three files share and none of them explains — it is not a description of a demographic, it is a specific individual receiving money from unconnected people in a coordinated rhythm. The timing correlation strengthens it, because coincidence does not usually keep a schedule. What this does not establish is what the money is for: three brothers supporting a parent, three employees paying an agent, or three contributors to a fund would all look like this. So the escalation states the connection, the timing and the absence of a declared relationship, and asks for the recipient to be checked against designations and adverse media — which is a question the institution cannot answer and somebody else can. That is the correct shape of a network escalation: a specific, non-demographic connection, handed to whoever holds the missing half. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Common counterparties across unconnected customers is the most productive network pattern in practice. — Funnel behaviour, shared identifiers and sequenced activity across accounts are the others worth knowing. — All of it requires cross-account visibility, which is infrastructure rather than analysis. — Much terrorist financing involves no network at all — a self-funded individual has nothing to connect. — A cell may share no financial relationship whatever, meeting only in the physical world. — You see your customers, their financial connections, and a retention window. Not other banks, not intent, not the real network. — The institution supplies a fragment, which makes the quality of the report matter more than the volume. 52

5.2.title: TWO REPORTS, SAME CASE
5.2.situation: Report A: 'Customer sends frequent small transfers to a high-risk jurisdiction and is a national of that country. Activity is consistent with terrorist financing typologies. Reported for review.' Report B: 'Between 3 March and 19 May the customer made eleven ATM withdrawals of €150–€250 across three cities (dates and locations listed), purchased two prepaid cards totalling €400 on 22 and 24 May, and on 26 May transferred €500 to [named individual, DOB, address, account, institution] in [country]. Asked on 2 June about the prepaid purchases, the customer first said they were gifts, then that they were for a family member abroad. No adverse media or designation match on the recipient. We could not establish the purpose of the withdrawals.'
5.2.question: What separates them?
5.2.answer: Report A gives the receiving unit nothing it can act on and one thing it should not have been given: nationality as a ground. It cannot be matched to anything, because it names nobody and dates nothing, and its stated basis describes several million people. Report B is usable in a specific way — the named recipient with identifiers can be checked against records the institution cannot see, the chronology can be compared against other reports on the same recipient, and the changed explanation is evidence obtainable only by the institution that asked. Note also what Report B does that analysts often omit: it records that the designation check came back clean, and states plainly what could not be established. That is not weakness in the report. It tells the reader exactly how far the institution got, which is what allows them to judge how much further they need to go. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The reporting threshold is effectively lower in TF: waiting for a case that satisfies an AML instinct means never reporting. — There is no de minimis, and speed matters because the report may concern an act that has not happened. — Attempted transactions are reportable in many jurisdictions and are often more informative than completed ones. — Identifiers are the joining material that lets your fragment be matched — and they are the part most often thinned. — Separate what you observed from what you infer, so the reader can tell your facts from your reading. — Demographic grounds give the reader nothing and consume capacity the useful reports need. — Reporting does not oblige you to close or freeze, and a closed account stops producing information. 61

1.2.title: THE SAME TRANSACTION, TWENTY YEARS APART
1.2.situation: Consider a single payment: a Swiss trading company pays a Dubai-based intermediary for a cargo of refined product, ultimately destined for a buyer in a country under sanction.
1.2.question: What does the compliance function actually have to do, under a comprehensive regime and under a targeted one?
1.2.answer: Under a comprehensive embargo the analysis is short. Is the destination the embargoed country? If yes, the transaction is prohibited regardless of the parties. The work is establishing destination, and the evasion problem is falsified documentation about where goods are going. Under a targeted regime the destination alone may prohibit nothing. The analyst must instead establish whether the Dubai intermediary is designated, whether it is owned or controlled by a designated party, whether the vessel carrying the cargo is listed or has been renamed, whether the ultimate buyer is designated, whether the product falls under a sectoral measure or a price cap, and whether any part of the payment chain creates a US nexus. Six questions instead of one, each requiring evidence, and five of them turning on identity rather than geography. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Comprehensive embargoes restricted whole economies and required little more than a country check. — UNSCR 661 (Iraq, 1990) was the last major comprehensive regime and the reason the approach was abandoned. — Targeted sanctions were designed through the Interlaken, Bonn-Berlin and Stockholm processes to move the cost onto decision-makers. — Screening as a discipline exists because of that shift. Naming parties created the identification problem. — The false positive is arithmetic, not a defect. Name matching is probabilistic where a country field was binary. 16

1.5.title: THE AID PAYMENT
1.5.situation: An international medical charity instructs a payment of $180,000 from its London account to a supplier in a country under comprehensive UN and national measures. The funds are for medical equipment destined for a field hospital. Your system alerts on the destination country and on the beneficiary bank, which is designated.
1.5.question: The purpose is plainly humanitarian. Is that a reason to release the payment?
1.5.answer: Not on its own — sympathy is not an authorisation. But it is a reason to establish whether an authorisation exists, which is a different thing. The analysis should identify whether the charity falls within the scope of UNSCR 2664 or an equivalent national general licence, whether the specific goods fall within the licensed categories, and whether the designated beneficiary bank is itself covered or excluded by the terms of that licence. A general licence that authorises humanitarian activity does not necessarily authorise routing it through a designated financial institution. The correct disposition is either a release under a named licence, with the licence identified in the rationale, or an escalation to establish whether a specific licence is required. What it is not is a release because the cause is good, or a block because the country is sanctioned. 23 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — De-risking withdraws service from entire categories and is treated by FATF, the FSB and the World Bank as a systemic harm. — Over-blocking is a compliance failure in its own right. Regulators do not treat it as a safe harbour. — UNSCR 2664 (2022) created a standing humanitarian exemption across UN asset-freeze regimes. — A humanitarian purpose may be an authorisation, not a mitigating factor. Identify the licence by name or escalate. — The measure of a screening function is how accurately it distinguishes, not how much it stops. 24 MODULE 2 Who imposes sanctions Sanctions come from several sources at once, and those sources do not agree with one another. This module covers the bodies that impose measures, the lists each maintains and what each list actually prohibits, when foreign law reaches an institution with no presence in that country, and what to do when two jurisdictions require opposite things. Most of the errors analysts make in their first year come from treating all of this as one list.

2.3.title: THE FIVE-YEAR LOAN TO A DIRECTIVE 1 BANK A
2.3.situation: European bank's syndication desk is arranging a five-year facility. One participant is a Russian financial institution that appears on the SSI List under Directive 1. The relationship manager notes correctly that the institution is not an SDN, that the bank maintains a correspondent account for it lawfully, and that payments to it have been processed without issue for years. The desk proceeds.
2.3.question: Is there a problem?
2.3.answer: Yes, and it is the exact prohibition Directive 1 exists to impose. New debt of longer than fourteen days' maturity for a Directive 1 institution is prohibited for US persons, and a five-year facility is squarely within it. Everything the relationship manager observed is true and none of it is relevant — the account, the payments and the absence of an SDN designation are all lawful and all beside the point. The specific question is whether this transaction is new debt above the maturity limit. Note also the second issue: whether the arrangement involves any US person, US dollar clearing or US-incorporated entity, because Directive 1 binds US persons. A purely European syndicate in euros raises a different question from one with a New York branch in it. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — SDN: full blocking. Property is frozen, reported within ten business days, and held until licensed. Returning funds is not blocking. — Machine-readable list formats carry identifying fields the human-readable versions drop. Screening a flattened extract discards what you need to discount. — SSI: not blocked. Each directive prohibits something narrow; everything else stays lawful. — CAPTA, Non-SDN MBS, NS-CMIC and FSE each carry tailored restrictions narrower than blocking. — The list — and for SSI the directive — must reach the analyst in the alert. Without it no disposition can be correct. — Disposition templates should differ by list. An SSI disposition that reads like an SDN one is evidence the distinction was not made. 33

2.4.title: THE EURO PAYMENT THAT WAS NOT OUTSIDE US REACH A
2.4.situation: German manufacturer instructs a euro payment from its German bank to a supplier in a third country. Neither party is a US person, the currency is not the dollar, and the goods were manufactured in Germany. Screening alerts because the supplier's beneficial owner appears on the SDN List. The analyst is preparing to record that no US nexus applies and that the payment should be assessed under EU measures alone.
2.4.question: What should the analyst establish before writing that?
2.4.answer: Several things, any of which would change the answer. Whether the German bank routes the payment through a correspondent that touches a US institution, which can happen even for euro payments depending on the correspondent chain. Whether the goods incorporate US-origin components or technology subject to US export jurisdiction. Whether any US person sits in the approval chain — a US-citizen relationship manager, a US-incorporated group entity providing the guarantee. Whether the manufacturer is a subsidiary of a US parent and whether the applicable programme reaches owned-or-controlled entities. If all of those come back negative, the conclusion is sound and should be written with the grounds stated. What is not acceptable is reaching the conclusion by noticing the currency and stopping. Note separately that the EU analysis is not the easier one here — the beneficial owner being designated raises the ownership and control question covered in Module 4, and the EU and UK tests differ. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — US person means citizens and permanent residents anywhere, US-organised entities including foreign branches, and anyone physically in the US. — Foreign subsidiaries of US parents are caught under the Iran and Cuba programmes but not most others. — A US-citizen employee approving a transaction engages in prohibited conduct personally, wherever they sit. — Secondary sanctions do not prohibit foreign parties. They create the risk that the foreign party is itself designated and loses dollar access. — Dollar clearing is the most common nexus: two non-US parties in dollars still touch a US correspondent. — The largest OFAC settlements involved non-US banks connected to the US only by dollar clearing, aggravated by stripping identifying data from payment messages. — State the nexus positively in the disposition, or state that none was identified and on what basis. Silence reads as not having asked. 36

2.6.title: THE INSTRUCTION YOU CANNOT LAWFULLY FOLLOW A
2.6.situation: French bank holds an account for an Iranian trading company. The company is not designated by the EU. It is designated by the United States, and the bank's US correspondent has indicated informally that maintaining the relationship is creating difficulty. The relationship manager proposes closing the account, citing commercial reasons, and asks compliance to confirm.
2.6.question: What is the compliance function's answer?
2.6.answer: Not a confirmation. The proposal is to terminate a relationship with a US-designated Iranian party, prompted by pressure connected to US measures — which is precisely the anticipatory compliance Bank Melli holds to be prohibited under the Blocking Statute. Citing commercial reasons does not help if the commercial reason is the US designation, and after Bank Melli the burden of demonstrating an unconnected reason falls on the bank. The correct handling is escalation to legal and senior management, with three questions on the table: whether a genuine and demonstrable commercial ground exists independent of the US measures, whether an authorisation from the Commission should be sought, and how the correspondent relationship is to be managed in the meantime. What the analyst records is the escalation and its grounds. What the analyst does not do is approve the closure, and does not record it as a routine de-risking decision. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Canada, Australia and Japan each maintain autonomous regimes; Canada's list is not a subset of anyone else's. — Switzerland aligns with EU measures regime by regime, as a decision each time rather than automatically. — Singapore is UN-focused by policy and treated its 2022 Russia measures as an explicit exception. — EU Regulation 2271/96 prohibits EU operators from complying with specified extraterritorial US measures, including by deliberate omission. — China's 2021 rules go further than blocking: they provide for counter-measures against parties that comply. — Bank Melli (2021): the prohibition bites without any US instruction, and an unexplained termination is treated as evidence of prohibited compliance. — Recognise and escalate. A conflict of laws is never an analyst-level disposition. 42 MODULE 3 Types of sanctions A designation tells you a party is restricted. It does not tell you what is restricted, and those are different questions. This module covers the measures themselves — asset freezes, the making-available prohibition, sectoral restrictions, trade and arms embargoes, dual-use controls, travel and transport measures, and restrictions on correspondent banking. An analyst who knows only that a name is listed can identify a hit but cannot dispose of one.

3.1.title: THE PAYMENT YOU RETURNED
3.1.situation: An inbound wire of $240,000 arrives for a corporate customer. Screening identifies the ordering customer as an SDN. The payment has been credited to a suspense account pending investigation. The operations team, wanting to resolve it quickly and avoid customer complaint, instructs the funds returned to the sending correspondent with the message 'unable to process'.
3.1.question: What has the institution done?
3.1.answer: Breached the blocking requirement, and probably compounded it. The funds came within the institution's possession, which means they were required to be blocked: placed in a blocked account, reported to OFAC within ten business days, and held until licensed. Returning them moved property in which a designated person had an interest, which is a prohibited dealing, and made funds available to the sending institution and ultimately back to the SDN. The message 'unable to process' also fails to tell the correspondent what happened, which in a chain of banks means the next institution may repeat the attempt. The correct handling was to block, report and notify internally — and the customer complaint, which was the thing the team was trying to avoid, is not a consideration that bears on the obligation at all. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Freezing immobilises. It is not confiscation, not account closure, and emphatically not returning the funds to the sender. — Returning a blocked payment is itself a prohibited dealing and destroys the evidence trail. — The making-available limb is broader than the freeze and is breached without touching a designated person's account. — Benefit is a factual test — a spouse's household expenses, a settled debt, a service provided. It cannot be automated. — Giving use of an asset is making it available even where title never moves. — US Fifty Percent Rule subsidiaries are blocked automatically and never appear on the SDN List. No list update will reveal them. — Blocked property is reported within ten business days in the US; rejected transactions are reported separately and are not the same event. 45

3.3.title: NINETY DAYS TO PAY A
3.3.situation: European industrial supplier sells equipment to a Russian energy company designated under a sectoral directive with a sixty-day new debt limit. The supplier's standard commercial terms are payment ninety days after delivery. The supplier's bank is asked to discount the resulting receivable. Nobody in the chain has treated the arrangement as a financing.
3.3.question: Is there a sectoral issue?
3.3.answer: Yes, and it exists before the bank is involved. Extended payment terms are an extension of credit and are treated as debt under these measures. Ninety-day terms to an entity subject to a sixty-day limit create new debt beyond the permitted maturity, which is prohibited for persons subject to the measure. The discounting compounds it rather than causing it. What makes this scenario worth studying is that everyone involved would describe the arrangement as ordinary commercial terms — no loan agreement exists, no interest is charged, and no one considers themselves a lender. The analyst's contribution is recognising that the legal test is the extension of credit and its tenor, not what the parties call it. The correct disposition escalates, and the correct commercial answer is to restructure to terms within the limit. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Sectoral measures restrict transaction types, not parties. The identity of the counterparty does not answer the question. — New means originated after the effective date, so the directive date matters as much as the designation date. — Debt is construed broadly: deposits, facilities, extended payment terms and deferred letters of credit are all capable of being caught. — Extended commercial payment terms are the most commonly missed form of prohibited new debt. — Service restrictions attach to project types, so the same entity may be lawful on one project and prohibited on another. — Professional services restrictions bite on advisory work rather than payments. — The price cap permits services below the cap and prohibits them above it. Compliance runs on tiered attestations, which is where the fraud is. 51

4.2.title: TWENTY-FIVE PER CENT, BLOCKED IN FULL
4.2.situation: Your customer is a Cyprus-registered trading company. Its shareholder register shows a single corporate shareholder, a Netherlands holding company, holding 100 per cent. The Netherlands company is 50 per cent owned by an individual designated last month and 50 per cent by an unconnected pension fund. A relationship manager argues the designated individual's ultimate economic interest in your customer is 50 per cent of 100, and that as this is not more than fifty per cent, and the pension fund holds the other half, the position is finely balanced but acceptable.
4.2.question: Is it?
4.2.answer: No, and the analysis contains two errors. First, 50 per cent is caught — the rule reads fifty per cent or more, so the Netherlands company is blocked outright, not finely balanced. Second, once the Netherlands company is blocked it is a blocked person, and it holds 100 per cent of your customer. Your customer is blocked in full. The pension fund's stake is irrelevant: it does not dilute the designated interest for these purposes, because the test at each level asks what proportion blocked persons hold, and at the level of your customer that proportion is 100 per cent. The pension fund's position is genuinely unfortunate — it holds an interest in a blocked entity through no fault of its own — but that is a matter for a licence application, not for the analysis of whether the prohibition applies. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Fifty per cent or more, in aggregate, directly or indirectly, by one or more blocked persons. — Exactly fifty is caught. Forty-nine is not, whatever the practical control. — The rule tests ownership, not control. OFAC urges caution on controlled entities but caution is not prohibition. — Each level is tested independently, so a blocked company's 50 per cent blocks the next entity — with no dilution as the chain lengthens. — UBO analysis multiplies down the chain; the Fifty Percent Rule does not. They give different answers and only one is the legal test. — Aggregation means one designated shareholder holding under half does not end the analysis. You need the whole register. — The rule does not run upwards to parents and does not reach sister companies laterally. Blocking those is unlawful denial of service. 65

4.3.title: THE GUARANTOR
4.3.situation: An EU customer is a mid-sized construction company. Its shares are held by two individuals with no designations, both of whom have run the business for fifteen years. A recently designated individual holds no shares, sits on no board and holds no office. He has, however, personally guaranteed the company's principal bank facility since 2019, and the guarantee remains in place.
4.3.question: Is the company caught by the EU test?
4.3.answer: Possibly, and on a limb most analysts do not have in mind. The ownership limb is not engaged — he owns nothing. But guaranteeing the entity's financial obligations is one of the Council's stated control indicators, and it is there precisely because standing behind a company financially is a form of control that leaves no trace in a shareholder register. The correct handling is to escalate, setting out the guarantee, its date and its scope, and noting the facts that cut the other way: the shareholders are independent and long-standing, the business predates the guarantee, and the guarantee was given years before the designation. That last point matters — a guarantee given in 2019 is not a post-designation arrangement and does not carry the circumvention indicators of one. Whether the indicator is displaced on those facts is a legal determination and not the analyst's. Recording both sides is. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The EU ownership threshold is more than 50 per cent; the US catches exactly 50. A 50-50 joint venture diverges. — Ownership may be direct or indirect, and the EU relies more on the control limb than on a prescriptive cascade. — Control has criteria, not a definition, and one may be enough depending on the circumstances. — Guaranteeing an entity's obligations is a stated control indicator — it catches a person who holds nothing and stands behind everything. — A finding of control can be rebutted on the facts, and the burden sits with whoever asserts independence. — Aggregation of minority holdings, and control mediated through a chain, are genuinely unsettled. — An escalation saying the position is unsettled is more useful than one manufacturing certainty. 68

5.4.title: NOTHING TO DISCOUNT ON
5.4.situation: Figure 5.1 is on your screen. A name score of 92 against an SDN entry. The list carries date of birth, place of birth, nationality and a passport number. The payment carries a name, an address in Dubai, and nothing else. The customer is a long-standing corporate importer and the payment is one of many similar ones.
5.4.question: What is the disposition?
5.4.answer: Not a discount, and not a block. Neither is supportable on what is in front of you. The list address is Khartoum and the payment address is Dubai, but address is weak for discounting — people move and hold property in several places — so that difference does not resolve it. The transaction looking ordinary is not evidence about identity and must not enter the rationale. The correct step is to seek the missing data: ask the customer for the beneficiary's full identifying details, or issue a request for information through the correspondent. If date of birth or a document number comes back and differs, the alert is resolved and the rationale records which identifier resolved it. If nothing comes back, the alert escalates with the position stated plainly — a strong name match, no secondary identifiers available on the payment side, information requested and not provided. That is a defensible record. 'Discounted, customer known to the bank' is not. 90 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The hierarchy: document numbers, then date of birth, then place of birth and nationality, then address, then title, then the name itself. — Work down from the strongest identifier present on both sides. An alert resolved on spelling is not resolved. — Dates of birth on sanctions records may be a year, a range or several alternatives — a range cannot be discounted by a single date. — 1 January appears far more often in real data than chance allows; it is frequently a placeholder. — Address is weak for discounting and strong for confirming, which is the reverse of how it is usually used. — A strong name match with no secondary identifiers cannot be resolved by analysis. Obtain information or escalate. — The transaction looking ordinary is not evidence about identity and does not belong in the rationale. 91

6.2.title: FOUR WEAK REASONS
6.2.situation: An analyst discounts an alert with the rationale: 'Beneficiary address is in Malaysia, list address is Yemen. Beneficiary described as a shipping agent, listed party described as a militia commander. Spelling differs by two characters. Customer has transacted with this beneficiary eleven times without issue. Discounted as a different party.'
6.2.question: Is the discount supportable?
6.2.answer: No, and each of the four reasons fails separately. The address difference is weak — the listed party's Yemen address is where they were recorded, not where they are. The occupation difference is not evidence: occupation is not verified on a sanctions record, and a militia commander using a shipping agent as a commercial identity is precisely the pattern these regimes exist to catch. The spelling difference is the reason the alert fired and cannot also be the reason it closes. The eleven prior transactions are a fact about the payment history, not about identity, and may mean eleven prior breaches rather than eleven prior confirmations. What is missing is any identifier: no date of birth, no document number, no place of birth. The correct disposition is to seek one and, failing that, to escalate. Note that the rationale is fluent, specific and detailed — which is what makes it dangerous. A reviewer skimming the queue may read length as rigour. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A discount is a positive finding that the parties differ, not a failure to confirm that they are the same. — The null discount — closed because nothing was found — is the most common finding in alert file testing. — Test your own work: complete 'this is a different person because…' with a fact, or you have not discounted. — Strong factors: differing document number, full date of birth, specific place of birth, documented nationality, established death. — A date of birth range cannot be discounted by a date inside it. — A different spelling is why the alert fired. It cannot also be why it closes. — Weak factors do not combine into a strong one unless they are genuinely independent. Four weak reasons usually means no strong one existed. 101

6.3.title: THE RIGHT DISCOUNT, OVERSTATED
6.3.situation: An alert fires on a beneficiary named Meridian Logistics Group against a designated entity named Meridian Logistics Ltd. The analyst obtains the beneficiary's registration certificate: incorporated in Singapore, registration number 201814927K, no connection to the designated entity, which is registered in Cyprus with a different number. The rationale reads: 'Confirmed different entity — Singapore registration 201814927K against Cyprus registration of the listed party. Entity is clear.'
6.3.question: What is wrong with an otherwise good piece of work?
6.3.answer: The analysis is correct and the last three words are not. Two different registrations in two jurisdictions is a strong identity discount and the sourcing is exactly right. But 'entity is clear' claims more than was established: the analysis addressed whether the beneficiary is the designated entity, and did not address whether the beneficiary is owned or controlled by designated persons — which would block it without any listing. The accurate closing sentence is 'confirmed not the listed entity; ownership not assessed'. That is a smaller claim and a defensible one. This matters beyond wording, because the next analyst to see this counterparty will read 'entity is clear' as covering ground it never covered, and the file will carry that error forward. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A differing registration number in the same jurisdiction is the strongest entity factor — confirm it is a registration and not a tax or licence number. — Groups operate near-identical names across jurisdictions by design, so jurisdiction distinguishes the legal person, not the group. — Compare the distinctive element of a name and discount generic tokens. Matching on holding, international and trading is matching on nothing. — Sector and line of business do not distinguish. List descriptions come from the designating authority, and front companies present ordinary business. — Substance and longevity are not evidence. Substantial companies are designated regularly. — A perfect identity discount leaves the ownership question entirely open. They are separate analyses on separate data. — Say what was established, not more. 'Not the listed entity; ownership not assessed' is accurate. 'Entity is clear' is not. 104

6.6.title: THE HOUR AFTER
6.6.situation: You confirm a true match on an inbound payment of $1.1m for a corporate customer. The ordering party is an SDN. The funds have been credited to your suspense account. Within twenty minutes the relationship manager calls: the customer is on the phone, the payment is for a shipment already loaded, and the customer wants to know what has happened so they can instruct the sender to resend from another account.
6.6.question: What do you do, and what do you say?
6.6.answer: The funds are in your possession, so this is a block rather than a rejection: they are moved to a blocked account, immobilised, and reported to OFAC within ten business days. They are not returned to the sender under any circumstances, and the customer's proposed remedy — resending from another account — describes circumvention and must be recorded rather than facilitated. On what to say: not that a sanctions match has been identified, not which party, not which list. The relationship manager is told that the payment is under review, that the customer should be told the same, and that any further communication will be issued by compliance after the position has been settled. The pressure will be considerable and the payment being for a loaded shipment does not change any of it. Escalate immediately, including the customer's suggestion, which is now a material fact in the file. 110 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Confirm against the publishing authority's own record before freezing. Extracts go stale and normalisation alters fields. — Block where the funds are in your possession; reject where they never arrived. The distinction is factual, not preferential. — Never return blocked funds to the sender — it is a prohibited dealing and puts money back with a possibly restricted party. — US: report blocked property and rejected transactions within ten business days, plus the annual 30 June return. — UK: report as soon as practicable; failure to report is a separate criminal offence. — Internal notification matters too. Discovering a frozen account from the customer is worse for everyone. — Do not tell the customer a payment was blocked for a sanctions match. That is not an analyst-level disclosure decision. — A customer proposing to resend from another account is describing circumvention. Record it; do not facilitate it. 111 MODULE 7 Vessel and maritime screening Most entry-level sanctions training treats vessels as a footnote. They are not: shipping is where the largest evasion networks operate, where the most sophisticated concealment happens, and where a bank's exposure sits in trade documents rather than in payment messages. This module covers vessel identity, what AIS does and does not tell you, the evasion techniques that have developed since 2022, the oil price cap, and what a financial institution can realistically check.

1.1.title: THE DOUBLE PAYMENT
1.1.situation: Delmar Credit pays its suppliers through an automated batch. During a month-end rush, a payments clerk, Anil Rao, releases a payment of GBP 4,800 to Castlegate Print Works twice, after the screen froze and he pressed the release button again. Castlegate’s accounts team does not report the second payment. Two months later a reconciliation finds it. Castlegate says the money arrived and was “applied to future work”. Anil says he has never worked with Castlegate staff outside the invoice process. A colleague suggests the loss should be written off as an operational error and the case closed.
1.1.question: Should the case be closed as an error?
1.1.answer: Not yet. The duplicate release looks like an error on Anil’s side, and nothing suggests he gained. But the supplier’s conduct is different. Castlegate received money it was not owed, did not tell Delmar, and now describes it as a prepayment. Whether that is an honest misunderstanding or a decision to keep the money depends on what Castlegate knew and when, and that has not been established. A sound practitioner records the loss as an operational error on the payment side, and separately asks for the overpayment back in writing. If Castlegate repays, the case closes cleanly. If it refuses or goes silent, the facts change and the case can be reassessed for dishonest retention. The common error is to treat the whole matter as a clerk’s mistake and never test what the recipient did once it noticed.

1.1.title: THE EARLY DEFAULT
1.1.situation: Larchmont Bank approves a personal loan for a new customer, Mara Voss, after an online application. Mara makes no repayments at all. The credit team writes the loan off as credit loss after the standard collection period. A fraud analyst later notices that the income stated on the application matches no pay records, that the employer’s phone number is a mobile that now rings out, and that the loan proceeds were moved on within a day to an account at another bank. The credit team says the file is closed and a write-off is a credit matter, not a fraud matter.
1.1.question: Is the credit team right that this is only credit loss?
1.1.answer: No. Credit loss describes a borrower who meant to repay and could not. Here the application contained statements that appear to be false, the evidence points to intent through the unreachable employer and the same-day movement of funds, and there is a clear benefit. That is deception, probable intent, loss and benefit, the four ideas from Topic 1.1.1. The write-off is an accounting step; it does not decide what the event was. A sound practitioner reopens the file as a suspected application fraud, records the evidence against each element, and asks whether other applications share the same employer or destination account. The loss should be reclassified in management reports too. The common error is to let the accounting treatment decide the risk classification. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — This guide uses four working ideas, which most fraud definitions combine in some form: deception, dishonesty or intent, loss or risk of loss, and benefit. — Fraud and error can cost the same; the difference is intent, which is inferred from repetition, concealment, benefit and failure to correct. — Use the word “suspected” until the evidence supports a label, because the label triggers freezes, database entries and staff action. — Theft takes property without deception, fraud obtains it by deception, laundering hides the origin of proceeds, and credit loss is honest non-repayment. — A defaulted loan that was obtained on false statements is fraud booked as credit loss, and misclassification hides the problem. — Preserve evidence for both criminal and civil routes, and do not wait for a prosecution before stopping loss. 16

1.2.title: THE MANAGER WHO NEVER TAKES LEAVE
1.2.situation: At Larchmont Bank, Hollis Grant has managed the supplier payments desk for eleven years. He has not taken more than two consecutive days off in all that time. He personally onboards new suppliers and is on first-name terms with several of them. A new internal auditor notes that Hollis seems under heavy pressure from a restructuring that may merge his desk with another. The head of operations says Hollis is the most loyal member of staff and that raising questions would insult him. No payment has been identified as wrong.
1.2.question: What should the auditor do?
1.2.answer: The auditor should recommend a review of the desk’s controls and recent supplier activity, not an investigation of Hollis. Several recognised flags are present together: leave avoidance, close supplier relationships, concentrated control over onboarding, and pressure. None proves anything, and the absence of a known wrong payment does not clear the desk, since a scheme that is working would not show up that way. A sound approach is to apply controls that do not depend on suspicion: enforce a period of continuous leave during which someone else runs the desk, separate supplier setup from payment release, and sample payments to recently added suppliers. That treats Hollis like everyone else and tests the process. The common error is to let loyalty or the fear of giving offence decide whether a control is applied.

1.2.title: THE FRAUD NOBODY COULD HAVE PREDICTED
1.2.situation: After a teller at a Delmar Credit branch is found to have diverted customer cash over several months, the review team meets. A senior manager says the case shows that fraud cannot be prevented: the teller had personal debts, no policy could have known about them, and the bank has no right to inspect staff finances. He proposes to close the review with a note that the loss was unforeseeable. The teller worked alone at the cash drawer and her work was never independently counted. She kept part of the cash from some customer deposits and entered a matching reversal on the till against each one, so her drawer balanced each day. Nobody else approved reversals.
1.2.question: Is the manager right that nothing could have been done?
1.2.answer: No. He is right that the bank could not have seen the pressure side, and wrong to stop there. The triangle has two other sides that the bank controls. Opportunity was wide: one person handled the cash with no independent count. Rationalisation is also open to influence through tone and consistent enforcement. The review should focus on opportunity because it is the side the firm can change. A sound review notes that the drawer balanced only because the same teller made the matching reversals, and introduces independent cash counts, dual approval of reversals and unannounced checks. The common error is to treat motive as the root cause when the cheapest fixes sit on the side the firm owns. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The fraud triangle, linked to Dr Donald Cressey, has three elements: pressure, perceived opportunity and rationalisation. — The fraud diamond, from Wolfe and Hermanson, adds capability, the traits and skills that let a person act on an opening. — The fraud pentagon is not used in this guide, so it is not tested here. — The models explain occupational fraud and are not predictive tools, so they must not be used to profile individuals. — The ACFE’s highest-loss red flags are excessive internal pressure, past legal problems, a close vendor or customer relationship, refusing vacation and a wheeler-dealer attitude. — A red flag justifies a review of controls and activity, never an accusation on its own. — Opportunity is the side of the triangle an institution controls most directly, so most preventive design targets it. 19

1.4.title: THE BRANCH MANAGER AND THE ALERT
1.4.situation: An analyst in the fraud operations team at Larchmont Bank notices that a series of small cash withdrawals from dormant customer accounts, all processed at one branch, were approved by the branch manager, Corin Ashby. The customers have not been contacted, and one of them is known to be abroad. There are about forty such accounts at the branch. Each withdrawal carries a signature that the branch holds on file. The analyst’s team leader suggests asking Corin directly whether he can explain them, since he is the person who knows the branch best.
1.4.question: Is asking the branch manager the right first step?
1.4.answer: No. The pattern suggests possible insider fraud, and the branch manager is the person who approved the transactions. Asking him first tells him that the activity has been seen, and he could remove or alter records. Investigating a possible insider should be done by a team independent of the line the person works in, usually the investigations function, with human resources and legal involvement as the firm’s policy requires. The analyst should record what was observed, limit who is told, and escalate to investigations under the insider-fraud procedure, which can check records and contact customers in a controlled way. In an insider case the line of reporting and the line of independence are not the same, and the analyst should follow the second. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — First-party fraud originates with the customer, third-party fraud with an outsider, and insider fraud with staff or trusted contractors. — A customer who authorises a payment after being deceived by a caller is the victim of third-party fraud, not a first-party fraudster. — Origin labels must follow the evidence and change when collusion or new facts appear. — Fraud overlaps with AML, cyber security, credit risk and operational risk, and early information sharing between these teams prevents silos. — Performance measures should be read in groups covering detection, efficiency, quality, customer impact and recovery, because one improving number can hide a worsening one. — In a descriptive three-lines view, fraud operations sit in the first line, fraud risk oversight in the second and internal audit in the third; this is an application of the model, not IIA wording. 25

1.5.title: THE TWO BIGGEST NUMBERS
1.5.situation: At the fraud committee of Delmar Credit, the head of fraud presents the quarter’s results. Gross loss to fraud, including the amounts the bank reimbursed to customers, was GBP 1,000,000. Recoveries from receiving banks and insurers were GBP 150,000, and customer reimbursements accounted for GBP 600,000 of the gross figure. A director argues that “the real loss is only GBP 400,000, because the bank refunded GBP 600,000 out of its fraud reserve rather than losing it”. The finance lead says the quarter’s net loss is GBP 850,000. The head of fraud is unsure which of them is right.
1.5.question: Which view of the loss is correct, and what is wrong with the director’s argument?
1.5.answer: On the definition in Topic 1.5.2, net loss is gross loss less recoveries, so GBP 850,000 is the net loss. The director has confused reimbursement with recovery. Reimbursements are part of the gross loss and part of the bank’s cost, not an offset to it. Money paid from a reserve is still money the firm has lost; the reserve only changes when the cost is recognised in the accounts. The head of fraud should present gross loss, recoveries, net loss and customer reimbursements as separate lines, each defined. Netting off money from any source other than a recovery shrinks the figure without shrinking the loss.

1.5.title: THE DECISION AT WEEK EIGHT
1.5.situation: It is the end of week eight at Larchmont Bank. Rhea Okonkwo has the second MI pack in front of her. It shows a low net loss for the instant-payments feature in the current month, which is incomplete, and a rise of almost threefold for the previous month, which is now complete. Attempts on the new feature are rising faster than on older channels. The contact centre has logged a theme of “safe account” calls. A colleague argues that the bank should wait for the current month to complete before deciding whether to tighten the controls, so that the decision is based on full data.
1.5.question: Should Rhea wait for the month to complete?
1.5.answer: No. The low current-month figure reflects late reporting, not safety, and the completed month already shows the trend. Attempts and complaint themes are leading indicators that are available now. Waiting for complete loss data means accepting another month of loss to gain precision the decision does not need. The cost of a temporary control, such as a short delay on first payments to new payees, is small compared with the growth the data already shows. Rhea should escalate with the evidence, propose time-limited controls with a review date and named measures, and mark the current month as provisional. Holding action until the lagging figure confirms what the leading figures already show would repeat the bank’s first-month mistake. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The four stages of the fraud lifecycle are prevent, detect, respond and recover, and what is learned in one case should feed the next prevention step. — Attempted fraud was stopped before loss, successful fraud caused a loss, gross loss is before recoveries and net loss is after recoveries. — Reimbursing a customer is how a firm bears a loss; it is not a recovery and does not reduce net loss. — A false positive is an alert on legitimate activity, and every false positive costs analyst time and causes customer friction. — Basis points of loss equal loss divided by volume, multiplied by 10,000, and the volume must match the loss. — Read an MI pack by checking definitions, denominators, period completeness, breakdowns and friction measures before the totals. — Recent periods in a fraud report are almost always incomplete, and leading indicators such as attempts and complaint themes should drive early action. 29 MODULE 2 The fraud risk management programme Fraud controls bought one at a time tend to protect last year’s problem. A programme is different: it is a set of connected decisions about who is accountable, which fraud risks matter, which controls answer them, how the results are measured and what happens when something goes wrong. This module teaches that structure. It follows the COSO and ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide, shows how to run a practical fraud risk assessment, explains control types, monitoring and the Three Lines Model, and ends with the UK offence of failing to prevent fraud, which turns good programme habits into a legal question. 30

2.1.title: THE TEAM THAT WAS THE PROGRAMME
2.1.situation: Larchmont Bank has a fraud operations team of twelve people, a modern transaction monitoring system and a quarterly fraud report that goes to the executive committee. The Chief Operating Officer tells the board that Larchmont has a complete fraud risk management programme and no further work is needed. When asked, nobody can show a board-approved statement of fraud risk appetite, a list of who is accountable for fraud in the lending and procurement functions, or a record of when the fraud risk assessment was last updated.
2.1.question: Does Larchmont have a fraud risk management programme in the sense used by the COSO and ACFE guide?
2.1.answer: Not yet. Larchmont has strong fraud operations, which is one part of control activity. A programme needs a communicated commitment from the board, a documented assessment of specific schemes, selected preventive and detective controls, a reporting and investigation process and monitoring of whether all of this works. The missing appetite statement, the missing accountability for lending and procurement fraud and the stale assessment show that the first two principles are not in place, and the card-and-payment focus shows that whole categories of fraud are unowned. 32 A sound analyst lists the five principles, record which are evidenced and which are not, and propose the first deliverables: a board-approved policy and appetite statement, named owners for each fraud category and a dated plan for the assessment. The common error is to treat a good detection team as proof that governance exists.

2.1.title: THE EXECUTIVE WHO WAIVED THE CHECK
2.1.situation: At Delmar Credit, a regional lender, the head of sales, Ravi Kapoor, is under pressure to hit a quarterly volume target. He instructs the underwriting team to skip the independent income check on loans from a favoured broker, saying the broker is trusted and the delay is costing deals. A junior underwriter, Mei Lin Tran, complies because Ravi sits two levels above her. Three months later, several of those loans default within weeks of drawdown.
2.1.question: What does this show about the control environment, and what would a sound programme have had in place?
2.1.answer: It shows a failure of the first principle in practice. A fraud policy and an income-check procedure existed, but a senior person could override the control without challenge, an incentive pushed towards cutting corners, and there was no route by which the junior underwriter’s concern would reach anyone with authority to act. Tone at the top was set by the instruction, not by the policy. A sound programme would require overrides of fraud controls to be approved in writing by someone independent of the sales line, logged and reported, would give staff a protected route to raise concerns, and would review whether the volume target itself rewarded risk. The common error is to blame the junior employee for complying instead of fixing the governance that made compliance the easiest course. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A fraud risk management programme is a joined-up set of governance, assessment, controls, reporting and review, not a single team or system. — The COSO and ACFE guide has five principles that mirror the five components of the COSO Internal Control Framework: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring. — The control environment principle requires a communicated programme that shows board and senior management commitment to integrity and ethics. — Risk appetite for fraud should be set openly by someone with authority, not silently by whoever tunes a rule. — A programme needs a senior owner across all fraud categories, an owner for each category and an owner for each control. — Overrides of fraud controls by senior staff are a direct test of tone at the top and should be approved independently, logged and reported. 33

2.2.title: THE REGISTER FULL OF MEDIUMS
2.2.situation: Fernlea Payments, a small payments firm, completes its first fraud risk assessment. The register has fourteen lines. Each is described by a category, such as “card fraud”, “account takeover” and “insider fraud”. Every inherent rating is medium for likelihood and medium for impact. Controls are listed as “fraud monitoring system” and “staff training” against every line. Residual ratings are all low, with the note “controls in place”. There are no owners, no test results and no actions. The head of compliance asks whether the register is ready to present to the board.
2.2.question: Is it ready? Identify the main weaknesses against the method in this chapter.
2.2.answer: It is not ready. The register stops at categories instead of schemes, so no control can be matched to a specific way of losing money. The uniform medium ratings suggest the ratings are not evidence-based and give the board nothing to prioritise. Residual ratings of low with “controls in place” are asserted, not reasoned. No owners or actions mean no risk response. A sound analyst sends it back with specific instructions: break each category into schemes, rate on evidence with written definitions, map and test controls per scheme, give reasons for residual ratings and add owners, responses and dates.

2.2.title: THE CONTROL THAT NEVER GOT TESTED
2.2.situation: Priya Nair, a risk analyst at Delmar Credit, is completing the assessment for the lender’s new online loan product. The scheme under review is synthetic identity applications, meaning applications built on a made-up identity assembled from real and false data. The product team says the risk is low because the application journey includes a document upload and a selfie check. Priya notes that no one has tested how the selfie check performs on poor-quality images, that the vendor supplied the pass rate in a sales document and that the document upload is not compared with any independent data. The product team asks her to enter the residual rating as low so that the launch date is kept.
2.2.question: How should Priya rate residual risk, and what should she record?
2.2.answer: She should not enter low. The controls exist, but the assessment’s job is to evaluate whether they work as designed, and none has been tested. The vendor’s figure is a claim, not a test result, and the document upload has no independent check behind it. On the evidence, the controls cannot be counted as fully effective, so residual risk should stay at the level the evidence supports, which on these facts is high, with a note saying why. A sound practitioner records the reasoning, proposes a response with an owner and date, such as testing the selfie check on realistic images and adding an independent data check, and escalates the request to keep the launch date to someone with authority to accept risk. If the business wants to launch, it can formally accept the residual risk, but that decision belongs to the right person and must be written down. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The assessment identifies specific schemes, not categories: who does what, exploiting which weakness, to gain what. — Inherent risk is the level with no controls; residual risk is what remains after the controls that actually work. — The six steps are identify schemes, rate inherent likelihood and impact, map and test controls, rate residual risk, decide the response and document. — A control that has not been tested should not be counted as fully effective. — The responses to residual risk are reduce, avoid, transfer or accept, and acceptance must be within appetite and approved by someone with authority. — The assessment is dynamic and iterative: refresh it on a schedule and whenever the product, partner, channel or threat changes. 36

2.3.title: THE ONE-SIZE-FITS-ALL PAUSE
2.3.situation: After a rise in invoice-redirection scams, in which customers are sent altered bank details for a genuine bill, Larchmont Bank introduces a 24-hour hold on every first payment to a new payee, whatever the amount or the customer. Scam losses on new payees fall. Within two months, complaints rise sharply, the contact centre is overwhelmed with calls about delayed rent and supplier payments, and a group of small business customers moves its accounts to a competitor. Meanwhile the fraud team finds that scam losses where details were changed on an existing payee have not fallen at all, because the hold never applies to them.
2.3.question: What does this show about the design of the control, and what would be a better approach?
2.3.answer: The control is blunt. It applies the same friction to every customer, so the cost falls mostly on honest customers making routine payments, while it covers only one route to the same loss. It reduced one pattern of loss at a high cost in experience and retention, left the neighbouring pattern untouched, and the cost was not measured when the control was designed. A better approach is proportionate friction. Hold or question only payments where signals raise risk, such as a new payee combined with an unusual amount, a change of details on an existing payee, a recent change of device or a customer in a call session. Add informative warnings, offer an easy route to confirm genuine urgent payments and monitor both fraud loss and the effects of friction.

2.3.title: TWO CONTROLS, ONE POINT OF FAILURE
2.3.situation: Delmar Credit protects its supplier payment run with two controls. First, a rule flags any change of supplier bank details for a manual call-back. Second, a monthly report lists all suppliers whose bank details changed during the month. Both controls draw on the same supplier master data table. In one month a supplier’s bank details are changed by someone with write access to the table, and neither control shows it: the rule does not fire and the monthly report lists no change. A large payment is made to the new account. The head of finance says the company had two independent controls.
2.3.question: Were the controls independent, and how should the design be improved?
2.3.answer: They were not. Both rely on the same master data table and its change history, so one successful manipulation defeated both. The institution had one control presented twice. Real independence needs a different source or a different person: for example, a report of bank detail changes taken from system audit logs that the data owner cannot edit, and a call-back to a contact number held separately from the master table. A sound practitioner also adds the missing structure around the table: restricted write access, dual approval for changes to bank details, and alerts on edits to the log itself. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Preventive controls stop a loss before it occurs, detective controls find it while or after it happens, and corrective controls limit harm and prevent repetition. — A scheme defended by only one type of control is fragile; look for prevention, detection and a corrective step. — Segregation of duties, authorisation limits and independent verification are structural controls that spread power and reduce single points of trust. — Verification is only independent if the source of the information is not controlled by the person asking for money. — Every control adds friction, so apply it in proportion to risk and measure the cost to legitimate customers as well as the fraud it stops. — Layered controls must be genuinely independent; two controls fed by the same data or person are one control. 39

2.4.title: THE DASHBOARD THAT ONLY SHOWED LOSS
2.4.situation: Fernlea Payments reports fraud to its board every quarter using a single chart of net fraud loss. For three quarters the chart has been falling, and the board congratulates the fraud team. The fraud lead, Tomas Reyes, privately knows that the false decline rate on genuine card payments has doubled since the team raised a rule threshold, that complaints about declined payments are rising and that a recently added monitoring feed has been failing intermittently, so some payments are not scored at all. None of this appears in the report.
2.4.question: What is wrong with the reporting, and what should Tomas do?
2.4.answer: The report presents one side of the picture. Falling net loss may reflect good control, but it may equally reflect unscored payments that were never recognised as fraud, or a tighter rule whose cost has been shifted onto genuine customers. A balanced set of metrics covers loss, control effectiveness, customer cost and response speed, and reports data-quality problems directly. Tomas should add the missing measures to the next report, describe the feed failure and its estimated exposure, propose a fix with an owner and a date, and explain that the fall in loss cannot be taken at face value until the feed is repaired.

2.5.title: AUDIT AS DESIGNER
2.5.situation: Fernlea Payments’ head of internal audit, Kwame Asante, is asked by the chief executive to help the fraud team design a new set of controls over supplier payments, because audit knows the process well. Kwame agrees, and his team writes the control descriptions and the testing approach. Six months later the board asks internal audit for assurance that the supplier payment controls are effective. Kwame proposes to assign the same auditor who helped design them.
2.5.question: Is this acceptable?
2.5.answer: No. The third line’s value rests on independence and objectivity. Having helped to design the controls, the auditor would be reviewing their own work, and the board could not treat the result as independent assurance. The model allows internal audit to give advice, but assurance on the same subject needs separation from the advice that shaped it. A sound approach is to have a different auditor, or an external reviewer, carry out the assurance work, and to tell the board about the earlier involvement. In future, audit’s advice should be given in a form that leaves management owning the design. It is the very reason independence is at risk. 44 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The IIA’s Three Lines Model describes roles: the governing body, a first line of management, a second line of specialist support and challenge, and a third line of independent internal audit. — The IIA document does not mention fraud, so the mapping of fraud to the lines is this guide’s own practical application, not IIA text. — In the practical mapping, the first line owns fraud risk and controls, the second line sets the programme and challenges, and the third line gives independent assurance. — The second line remains part of management, so it is not independent in the way the third line is. — Common failures are a first line that disowns fraud, a second line that becomes the operator, a second line too weak to challenge and a third line drawn into design. 45

2.6.title: THE BROKER AND THE FALSE CLAIM
2.6.situation: Delmar Credit, a large lender, pays commission to independent brokers who introduce borrowers. A broker, Stefan Brandt, tells borrowers that Delmar’s loans carry no early repayment charge, which is untrue, so that more of them sign. No one at Delmar’s senior level knew. Delmar’s fraud risk assessment covers customer application fraud and staff theft, but has no entry for fraud by brokers against borrowers for Delmar’s benefit. When complaints reveal the pattern, Delmar’s lawyers ask whether the lack of senior knowledge protects the company.
2.6.question: Does the absence of senior management knowledge protect Delmar, and what does the assessment gap suggest?
2.6.answer: No, not on that ground alone. The offence is framed around the associated person’s fraud and the organisation’s failure to prevent it, not around what senior managers knew. If Stefan provides services for Delmar, and the fraud was intended to benefit Delmar as well as himself, the question becomes whether Delmar can prove reasonable prevention procedures. Whether the offence applies is a legal judgement, and Chapter 7.1 gives the detail. 47 The assessment gap is the key weakness. The risk assessment principle asks the organisation to assess fraud by associated persons for its benefit, and due diligence asks for checks on them. Delmar did neither for brokers. A sound response is to add the scheme to the register, introduce due diligence, training and sampling for brokers, and take legal advice on the present case. Assuming that not knowing is a defence is the wrong lesson.

2.6.title: THE OVERSEAS AGENT AND THE REASONABLE STEPS
2.6.situation: Fernlea Payments, a large payments firm, uses an overseas agent network to sign up merchants. A sales director, Hana Okafor, learns that one agent has been telling merchants that Fernlea guarantees settlement within an hour, which is untrue, and that merchants signed up on that basis. Fernlea has a written fraud policy, annual staff training for employees only, and no risk assessment of agents. A colleague says that because the agent is a separate company, Fernlea cannot be responsible.
2.6.question: Is the colleague right, and what does the case say about reasonable procedures?
2.6.answer: The colleague is wrong to treat separateness as protection. An associated person includes an agent and anyone providing services for or on behalf of the organisation, and the fraud appears to have been committed to benefit Fernlea as well as the agent. Whether the offence is made out is a legal judgement, but the structure of the offence makes Fernlea’s own procedures the central question. On the facts, Fernlea would struggle to show reasonable procedures: no assessment of agent risk, training limited to employees and no due diligence or monitoring of the network. A sound response is to take legal advice now, stop the misstatement, assess the agent risk, add due diligence, contractual terms and training for agents, and monitor merchant complaints. Relying on corporate separateness, instead of asking what prevention procedures existed, is the trap. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The UK offence of failure to prevent fraud applies to a large organisation when an associated person commits a specified fraud offence intending to benefit the organisation. — The offence is framed around the failure to prevent an associated person’s fraud, not around what senior managers knew; Chapter 7.1 gives the detail. — An associated person includes an employee, an agent, a subsidiary and others who provide services for the organisation, judged on all the circumstances. — The defence is that the organisation proves it had reasonable prevention procedures, or that it was not reasonable to expect any; the burden is on the organisation. — The six guidance principles are top level commitment, risk assessment, proportionate procedures, due diligence, communication including training, and monitoring and review. — The guidance is advisory and not a safe harbour, and the offence targets fraud that benefits the organisation, not customer reimbursement. 48 MODULE 3 External fraud External fraud is fraud committed by people outside the institution against its customers, its products or its payment rails. This module settles how each major type runs, what it looks like from inside the institution, and which controls realistically work. Chapters 3.1 to 3.3 cover scams where the customer is tricked into paying, takeovers where the criminal acts as the customer, and the mule accounts that receive the proceeds of both. Chapters 3.4 to 3.7 then cover card fraud, identity, application and first-party fraud, business email compromise and corporate payment fraud, and cheque, deposit and other payment fraud. Every later module assumes this vocabulary. 49

3.1.title: THE CALM CUSTOMER WITH A SCRIPT
3.1.situation: Maribel Okafor, a retired customer of Larchmont Bank, has used mobile banking for years to pay small bills. On a Tuesday morning she tries to send nearly all of her savings to a new payee at another bank, with the purpose “family help”. The application records that she has been on a call for the whole session and that she copied the account details from her messages. The payee name does not match the account name. A payment-hold analyst, Tomasz Reyes, phones Mrs Okafor, who says she is happy and in a hurry, that nobody told her to do this, and that she does not want the bank interfering.
3.1.question: Should Tomasz release the payment because the customer is calm, consistent and insists it is her own decision?
3.1.answer: No. Her calm and insistence do not outweigh the signals: a first-ever payment of this size, the draining of savings, a new payee whose name does not match, a call running throughout the session and a payment purpose that does not fit her history. Coached victims commonly say what Mrs Okafor said, because the fraudster has rehearsed it with them. A sound practitioner keeps the payment held, within whatever the institution’s terms allow, and moves from yes-or-no questions to open ones: who is the payee, how did you meet them, who else knows. If the customer still cannot explain, the case goes to a specialist, and the bank considers contacting a trusted contact where the customer has nominated one. The aim is to give the customer a moment away from the voice on the other line.

3.1.title: A WARNING FOR EVERY PAYMENT
3.1.situation: Delmar Credit, a small payments firm, adds the same warning to every outgoing faster payment: “Be aware of scams. Only pay people you trust.” Many Delmar customers pay the same few people every week, so most of them see the same words several times a month. After six months the fraud team finds that most customers who later reported scams had clicked through the warning in a couple of seconds, and the warning has not changed the number of scam reports. The team can also see which payments were to new payees and which were not. The head of operations, Priya Nair, proposes to make the warning longer and to add a second tick-box confirmation on every payment.
3.1.question: Is a longer warning with a second tick-box the right fix?
3.1.answer: No. The evidence shows that the generic warning has been learned and ignored, and adding more text and another tick-box to every payment will teach the same habit faster while irritating genuine customers. Friction applied equally to all payments is poor design because it does not match the warning to the risk. The better answer is to target. Ask for the payment purpose, use it to show a short warning about the matching scam type, and reserve slower steps, such as a delay or a staffed conversation, for payments with several risk signals. Delmar should then measure whether the targeted warnings change what customers do, using the outcomes of held payments and later reports, and adjust. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — An APP scam is a payment the customer genuinely authorised after being deceived, so the usual test of whether the customer made the instruction does not separate it from a legitimate payment. — The two families are malicious payee, where the payee is the fraudster, and malicious redirection, where the customer intends to pay a genuine party or their own bank. — Scams can be described in five stages, and the institution has clear evidence only in the last two, so behaviour and context must carry the detection. — Urgency, authority, trust and isolation are the levers, and coaching the victim to give a false payment purpose is the fraudster’s defence against bank questions. — Red flags fall into payment behaviour, session behaviour and customer behaviour, and no single one proves a scam; the combination does. — Controls work in layers: tailored warnings, dynamic friction, payee checks, holds where permitted and trained staff, with generic warnings on every payment the weakest of these. 53

3.2.title: THE CALLER WHO SOUNDS RIGHT
3.2.situation: At Larchmont Bank, a caller says she is Hana Verlaan and has lost her phone. She sounds distressed and gives her full name, address and date of birth correctly.
