She asks the contact-centre agent, Ravi Menon, to change the mobile number on her account to a new one and to send a new security code there. The agent’s screen shows that the account had a password-reset request two hours earlier, from a device not seen before. The caller says she is in a hurry because she needs to pay a deposit that afternoon. The agent finds her voice natural and her answers confident.
3.2.question: What should Ravi do?
3.2.answer: He should not change the number on the strength of the call. The details the caller gave are the kind that appear in data breaches and on social media, so correct answers do not prove identity. The earlier password reset from an unknown device, followed by a request to change the contact number and urgency about a payment, matches the first three phases of a takeover. Ravi should follow the institution’s recovery procedure, which should require a stronger check than knowledge of personal details, such as an in-branch visit, document verification or a call-back to the number already on file. He should tell the fraud team about the earlier reset. If the genuine customer has lost her phone, a short delay costs little. If the caller is a criminal, the delay may protect the whole balance.

3.2.title: TWO REPORTS, ONE MORNING
3.2.situation: Two customers of Delmar Credit report losses on the same morning, and the intake clerk has a long queue and a template that offers only two choices, authorised or unauthorised. Customer one, Idris Cole, says he did not make a payment at all: his phone stopped working the previous evening, and when he got a replacement he found transfers out of his account. Customer two, Tilly Brandt, says a caller from “the fraud department” asked her to install a program so they could “check her security”, watched her screen for twenty minutes, and she later found money gone. The intake clerk proposes to log both as unauthorised because neither customer typed a payee.
3.2.question: Is the clerk’s classification sound for both?
3.2.answer: Not for both. Mr Cole’s pattern fits a takeover, possibly through a SIM swap, and it is reasonable to treat his payments as unauthorised pending the investigation. Ms Brandt’s case cannot be logged as unauthorised on the intake facts alone: she enabled remote access after a deception, so it is a mixed case and must go to a trained investigator before it is classified. Labelling both as unauthorised on the basis of “no one typed a payee” confuses who pressed the keys with who was deceived. The right step is to record the facts in each customer’s own words before classifying, then pass both cases to a trained investigator who knows the applicable rules. The classification can be refined later; the first hours cannot be recovered. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Account takeover means a criminal acting as the genuine customer, so the payments are generally unauthorised and the loss rules differ from scams. — A takeover runs in four phases: obtain access, test, lock in by changing contact details or devices, and cash out. — Read the sequence, not the single event; a reset, a new device, a profile change and a new payee in a short window together are a strong signal. — Strong customer authentication makes stolen details alone insufficient, but it does not stop a customer who is tricked into reading out a code, and phishing-resistant authenticators address that gap. — Account recovery, password reset and contact-detail change must be at least as well protected as login, and staff are part of the authentication chain. — A convincing voice, face or set of personal details is not proof of identity, and deepfakes weaken them further. — Establish the facts in the customer’s own words before classifying a case as unauthorised or authorised, because mixed cases such as remote access exist. 57

3.3.title: THE BUSY SHOP ACCOUNT
3.3.situation: Larchmont Bank’s monitoring flags a business account held by Dev Kapoor, who sells second-hand bicycles online. Over one week the account received credits from many unrelated senders and sent most of the money onward within hours, mainly to two payees and as cash withdrawals. The analyst, Sofia Marchetti, notes that the account is only a few weeks old and that the stated turnover on opening was small. A colleague argues that many payers and fast onward payments are the mule pattern, so the account should be treated as a mule account now.
3.3.question: Is the pattern enough to conclude that this is a mule account?
3.3.answer: No, not yet. Many unrelated payers and quick onward payments are the mule pattern, but a small online trader can show the same flow: customers pay in, and the trader pays suppliers and withdraws cash. What separates the two is whether the activity fits a lawful purpose. Here the thin history and the gap between stated and actual turnover raise the risk, yet they do not prove it. Sofia should test the explanation against the evidence. She can look at payment references, whether the inbound payers look like customers or like victims, whether the onward payees are suppliers, and whether any inbound payment has been reported as fraud by another bank. A conversation with Mr Kapoor and a request for trading records would settle most of it. A limited restriction is justified while the question is open, but labelling him a mule before checking is not.

3.3.title: THE FAVOUR FOR A FRIEND ONLINE
3.3.situation: Camille Duarte, a student, tells a fraud analyst at Delmar Credit that for two months she has been messaging a man she met on a dating app. He says his own bank account is frozen and that his customers abroad need to pay him, so he asks her to receive their payments and forward most of the money to another account, and she keeps a small share as thanks. She says he has been kind and consistent, she has never met him, and she assumed the payers were his customers. Her account shows several unrelated senders a week and fast onward transfers. The analyst’s manager says Camille should be recorded as a deliberate mule and the account closed, because she took a share and the pattern is textbook.
3.3.question: Is the manager’s conclusion sound?
3.3.answer: It goes too far. The pattern is consistent with mule activity, and the account is clearly a risk, but the evidence of what Camille knew points toward an unwitting or, at most, partly aware participant who has been drawn in through a romance story and is likely a victim herself. A share of the money does not by itself prove knowledge, because recruiters offer small rewards so that the arrangement feels like a favour. Recording her as a deliberate mule needs evidence of what she knew, and two months of friendly messages and a plausible story are evidence of recruitment, not of guilt. The sound course is to restrict the account so no further proceeds pass through, take her account of events in full, pass the recruiter’s details and the onward accounts to the financial crime team, and give her clear information about what to stop doing. The decision on closing the account and on any report belongs to the people designated to make it. Camille is a risk to the institution and is likely also a victim, and the process should protect both interests. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A money mule is someone who moves money for another person, and a mule account is any account used to receive and move proceeds of crime. — Mules are witting, unwitting or complicit, and the difference is the knowledge they had, which is found by talking to them, not by looking at a screen. — Accounts become mule accounts in four ways: opened for the purpose, genuine accounts used by arrangement, taken-over accounts, and victims turned mules. — The core flow is many unrelated payers in, fast pass-through, and exit by transfer, cash or conversion; pass-through speed and counterparty spread separate a mule from a busy honest account. — Mule activity is where fraud and money laundering meet, so the facts must pass between the two teams quickly, and the reporting detail sits in Chapter 6.5. — Treat the account as a risk and the person as a possible victim: restrict the account, ask open questions, record the evidence and decide on closure and reporting at the right level. — Speed is the main control, because a mule account is valuable to a criminal only while it can pass money on. 62

3.4.title: WHO PAYS FOR THE ONLINE ORDER
3.4.situation: Calder Bank issued a credit card to a customer, Mr Haldane. A criminal used the card details to order electronics from an online shop, Brightside Gadgets, which sells through an acquirer, Tarn Payments. Brightside’s checkout offers cardholder authentication through 3-D Secure, but it was switched off for this order because the shop considered it a source of abandoned baskets. Calder approved the payment. Mr Haldane saw it a week later, denied making it, and Calder raised a chargeback with a fraud reason code. Brightside says the order looked normal and asks Tarn to contest the chargeback because the goods were delivered.
3.4.question: On the general scheme logic, who is most likely to bear the loss, and why does delivery not settle it?
3.4.answer: The loss most likely falls on Brightside through Tarn. The order was unauthenticated even though authentication was available, so the merchant side most likely did not use the protection that would have moved fraud liability towards the issuer. Delivery to someone does not show that the genuine cardholder made the purchase. In a fraud dispute the question is whether the cardholder authorised the payment, and a delivery to a criminal’s address proves nothing against that. A sound view for Tarn is that Brightside’s choice to switch authentication off was a business decision with a price. Tarn can still help the merchant respond if it has real evidence tying the order to the cardholder, such as a long account history, but it should also review Brightside’s controls, since a merchant that disables protection tends to attract fraud and disputes.

3.4.title: THE DISPUTED PARCEL
3.4.situation: Priya Nair at Delmar Credit reviews a fraud dispute from a cardholder, Mr Osei. He says he did not make an online purchase of sports equipment last month. Delmar’s records show that the order was placed from the phone Mr Osei has used for two years, authenticated by his banking app, and delivered to his home address, where he has received six earlier orders from the same retailer. This is his third fraud dispute in five months, each on a delivered order. Mr Osei says that he has been a loyal customer for years and that Delmar should simply refund him.
3.4.question: How should Priya treat the dispute?
3.4.answer: The evidence points towards a first-party dispute rather than third-party fraud. The device, the authentication, the delivery address and the purchase history all tie Mr Osei to the order, and the repeated pattern of disputes on delivered goods is a recognised warning sign. None of those signs is conclusive alone, but together they support refusing to treat the claim as third-party fraud: Priya should refer it for first-party review and not pay it as third-party fraud unless that review finds a credible explanation. Priya should not accuse Mr Osei of anything on the call. She should record the evidence, give him a fair chance to explain, for example whether a household member used the phone, and apply the bank’s process. If the pattern is established, the case should be referred to the first-party fraud team, and any record shared with other lenders must meet the evidential standard described in Topic 3.5.6 and Chapter 6.5. The error to avoid is a quick refund that rewards the behaviour, or a quick accusation that ignores the chance of an innocent explanation. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A card payment involves five roles: cardholder, merchant, acquirer, scheme and issuer, and each holds different evidence and different controls. — Physical card fraud covers lost and stolen, counterfeit and cards not received, while card-not-present fraud uses only the card details and is judged by context. — Card testing shows as bursts of small attempts, many card numbers from few sources and a high decline rate with a repeated reason. — Tokenisation reduces the value of stolen data, and authentication such as chip and PIN, 3-D Secure and strong customer authentication checks the payer, but neither stops a customer who is deceived into approving a payment. — A chargeback moves a loss back through the scheme, and liability depends on scheme rules about authentication and technology used, not on whether goods were delivered. — Friendly fraud is a working term for a dispute by the genuine cardholder, and honest mistakes must be separated from deliberate misrepresentation by evidence. 66

3.5.title: THE CUSTOMERS WHO SHARED A FLAT
3.5.situation: Larchmont Bank opens credit card accounts for three new customers within two weeks. They have different names and credit histories of moderate length, but their applications give the same mobile number with one digit changed, and the delivery addresses are two flats in the same building. Over the next four months each account is used lightly and paid on time, and each requests a limit increase, which Larchmont grants. In month five all three accounts reach their limits within three days, mostly through purchases of high-value goods, and the payments stop. Larchmont’s collections team assumes three unrelated customers hit hard times.
3.5.question: What does the pattern suggest, and what should the bank have done earlier?
3.5.answer: The pattern suggests a bust-out, probably across linked identities that may be synthetic. The signs were present from the start: near-identical contact details, nearby delivery addresses and simultaneous applications. The quiet period of on-time payments built credibility so that limit increases would be granted, and the final burst used the limits fully before default. Treating the three accounts as unrelated customers in difficulty is the tempting and wrong reading. The earlier opportunities were at application, where linked-application checks on shared contact data would have flagged the group, and at limit increase, where a policy of caution for thin or new relationships would have capped the exposure. Now, Larchmont should treat the cases as fraud and not collections, review whether other accounts share the same links, and consider a report to the appropriate authority and, where permitted, to fraud-sharing databases. The decision rules for reporting are in Chapter 6.5.

3.5.title: THE HIT THAT WAS NOT PROOF
3.5.situation: Merrow Lending screens a new loan application against a fraud-sharing database. The result shows a record filed two years ago by another lender, noting a false application. The applicant, Mr Adebayo, explains that the earlier record related to an application in which his employer’s name was entered wrongly by a broker, and that he has since asked the other lender to review it. Everything else in Mr Adebayo’s application checks out: identity, address, income, device and employer, which Merrow has confirmed by calling the employer’s payroll office. The junior analyst proposes to decline automatically because there is a database hit.
3.5.question: Is an automatic decline the sound decision?
3.5.answer: No. A database hit is evidence that another member held a concern, not proof that the present application is fraudulent. Although the filing standard is demanding, Mr Adebayo has raised a specific, credible challenge, and everything else in this application is verified. Declining automatically would make the database the decision-maker and would risk an unfair outcome. A sound analyst treats the hit as a flag that requires review. Merrow should assess the application on its own evidence, consider asking the filing lender whether the record is under review, apply a cautious approach such as extra verification, and document the reasoning. If Merrow does decline, the reason should be one it can explain and defend, and Mr Adebayo should know how to pursue the challenge with the filing member. 69 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Identity theft uses a real person’s identity without consent, while synthetic identity fraud fabricates a person, often by combining real and invented data, and so produces no complaining victim. — Application fraud has a third-party form, using another person’s or a fabricated identity, and a first-party form, in which the genuine applicant lies about their own circumstances. — A bust-out builds credibility and then uses the limits fully with no repayment, and loan stacking exploits the lag before other lenders can see new debt. — First-party fraud is a working term for deceit by the genuine customer, and the hardest question is intent, so reports should state what the evidence shows and not a conclusion about guilt. — A consortium hit is an input to a decision and not a verdict, because filing standards, accuracy and the right to challenge are part of how a shared database stays fair. 70

3.6.title: THE SUPPLIER WHO CHANGED BANKS
3.6.situation: Weaver and Pike, a small construction firm, receives an email from the accounts office of its steel supplier, Ardent Metals, saying that its bank has changed and giving new account details for the next invoice. The invoice is for a larger amount than usual because of a bulk order, and the project manager is waiting for the delivery. The email address is almost identical to the usual one. The accounts clerk, Sunil, phones the number at the bottom of the email, speaks to a polite person who confirms the change, and releases a large payment. A week later the real Ardent Metals chases the unpaid invoice.
3.6.question: What went wrong in the verification, and what should the process have required?
3.6.answer: The verification failed because it used the channel the criminal controlled. The phone number came from the email, so the polite person who confirmed the change was part of the scheme. The near-identical sender address was a warning sign that went unnoticed, and a change of bank details just before a large payment was exactly the trigger that should have forced independent checking. The process should have required Sunil to call a number held on file before the request, such as the number in the original supply contract or a previous genuine invoice, and to speak to a known contact. A second person should have approved any change to payee details, and the first payment to new details should have been held until verified.

3.6.title: THE URGENT TRANSFER FROM THE MANAGING DIRECTOR
3.6.situation: At Larchmont Bank, a payments analyst, Tomás Herrera, sees a transfer from Orlin Foods, a food manufacturer, to a beneficiary at a bank in another country that Orlin has never paid before. The amount is several times the company’s usual supplier payment. The beneficiary account was opened a few days ago, and the payee name check returned an exact match to the name typed in. The finance clerk, Ahmed, released the payment with his own credentials, and a colleague approved it within minutes without a call. A note on the payment reads “per MD, confidential, pay today”. The managing director is known to be abroad. A colleague tells Tomás that an exact match and two approvals mean the payment is safe, and that holding it would annoy a good customer.
3.6.question: What should Tomás do?
3.6.answer: Tomás should hold the payment and contact the customer through details already on file, and not through the instruction. An exact match shows only that the typed name agrees with the account name, not that the account holder is the intended payee. The two approvals do not help, because the second was given within minutes without an independent check. The facts that matter are a new beneficiary abroad, an account opened days ago, an unusual amount, secrecy and urgency, and an executive who cannot be reached. Together they match executive impersonation. 74 The cost of a short delay and a call is small beside the cost of an unrecoverable payment. If Orlin’s finance director confirms through the verified route that the payment is genuine, Tomás releases it and notes why. If Orlin did not expect it, the payment is stopped and the case becomes a BEC investigation. The error to avoid is treating a good history, a clean name check and two approvals as proof that the instruction is real. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — BEC is the use of compromised or impersonated email to cause payments, and email account compromise is the same method aimed at individuals’ personal email. — The two technical routes are control of a genuine mailbox and impersonation through a forged name or lookalike domain. — Vendor impersonation changes where a real invoice is paid, and executive impersonation demands an urgent and secret payment, but both exploit a process that accepts an unverified instruction. — Out-of-band verification confirms an instruction through a channel that the instruction itself did not supply, using contact details held before the request. — A bank’s payments team can warn, offer dual authorisation and payee verification, detect new or young beneficiaries and close name matches, and act fast with the receiving bank. — A corporate customer controls the most important defences: callbacks on any bank-detail change, separation of duties, multi-factor authentication on email and a culture in which pausing a payment is rewarded. 75

3.7.title: THE OVERPAID SELLER
3.7.situation: Ms Rao, a customer of Larchmont Bank, is selling a second-hand piano online. A buyer from another city sends her a cheque for much more than the asking price, saying that the extra covers a courier whom Ms Rao should pay from her account once the cheque clears. She deposits the cheque at a branch machine, sees the full credit on her account within the hour, and asks the branch to send the extra by transfer to the courier. The teller notes that the credit is showing and that the customer is calm and polite.
3.7.question: What should the teller do, and why does the visible credit not settle the question?
3.7.answer: The teller should pause and ask about the transaction. A cheque for more than the price, with the balance to be sent to a third party, is the textbook shape of an overpayment scam. The credit is provisional: the paying bank has not yet confirmed the cheque, and if it is returned as counterfeit the credit will be reversed. The money Ms Rao sends would then be her own. A sound teller explains in plain words that the credit does not mean the cheque is good, advises her not to send funds until the item has finally cleared, and escalates the case so that the deposit is examined and a hold or a return can be applied.

3.7.title: THE NEW CHANNEL QUESTIONS
3.7.situation: Larchmont Bank plans to launch an instant person-to-person payment feature in its mobile app. The product team argues that fraud risk is low because the feature is only for customers who already have accounts and who log in with a fingerprint. Payments up to a generous limit will be instant and final, and the app will not show any warning before sending. New payees can be added in the app within seconds. The product team wants to launch within a month and sees fraud controls as something to add later if problems appear. The fraud team is asked for its view in a short meeting.
3.7.question: Using the four questions about new channels, what should the fraud team say?
3.7.answer: The fraud team should say that the risk is not low, and should walk through the four questions. Customers are identified by a fingerprint on a registered device, which protects against a stranger but not against a customer who is tricked into sending money. A payment is authorised by the customer alone, so a scam victim authorises it willingly. It becomes final at once, so there is no later chance to recall it. And nobody sees the full picture unless the bank builds real-time monitoring and payee checks. A sound recommendation is to launch with a lower initial limit, a payee check or warning for new payees, real-time monitoring of unusual patterns and a clear route for customers to report quickly. The limits can rise as the data shows how the channel behaves. 77 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A cheque is credited before it is confirmed, and that gap between funds shown and funds final is what most cheque and deposit fraud exploits. — UK Finance describes three types of cheque fraud: counterfeit cheques on non-bank paper, forged signatures on genuine cheques, and genuine cheques fraudulently altered after writing. — Overpayment scams and remote deposit abuse use provisional credit, and the signs are in the story, such as an overpayment and a request to return the balance. — Kiting uses the delay in clearing across accounts to create balances backed by no real funds, and circular movement between the same accounts is its sign. — New channels carry old frauds at higher speed, so ask how the customer is identified, how payment is authorised, when it is final and who sees the whole picture. 78 MODULE 4 Internal and third-party fraud Most of this guide looks at fraud that arrives from outside the institution. This module looks at fraud that is carried out by people who already have a badge, a login or a contract. Employees, contractors, vendors, brokers, agents and outsourced teams all sit inside the control perimeter, and they know how the controls work. That knowledge is what makes them dangerous. The module teaches the standard classification of occupational fraud, the common employee and vendor schemes and the controls that stop them, the particular risks of insiders in banks and payments firms, the risk that comes with outsourcing, and the reporting channels that detect more of these frauds than any other method. 79

4.1.title: WHICH BRANCH OF THE TREE
4.1.situation: Brightwater Credit, a fictional consumer lender, finds that Rohan Mistry, a procurement manager, has been awarding printing contracts to Kestrel Print, a firm owned by his brother-in-law. Kestrel’s prices are well above the market rate. A review also finds that Rohan has approved invoices from Kestrel for jobs that were never delivered. The invoices were paid from the marketing budget. Nothing is missing from any bank account; every payment was authorised in the ordinary way and every reconciliation balances. The internal audit team asks how the case should be classified in its report.
4.1.question: Under the ACFE classification, which branches of occupational fraud does the case involve?
4.1.answer: It involves two branches. The undisclosed ownership link and the inflated prices are corruption: a conflict of interest, and probably a kickback or at least a favoured supplier whose benefit passes to the manager’s family. The invoices for undelivered work are a billing scheme, which sits under fraudulent disbursements and therefore under asset misappropriation. The ACFE counts a case under each branch it touches, so the report should record both. The tempting conclusion is that there is no fraud because “the books balance and every payment was approved”. That confuses an accurate ledger with an honest transaction. Reconciliation proves that money left the account as recorded, not that the goods existed or the price was fair. A sound analyst would look for proof of delivery on each invoice, compare Kestrel’s prices with other suppliers, and ask who disclosed the family tie and who should have been told.

4.1.title: THE COLLEAGUE WHO NEVER TAKES LEAVE
4.1.situation: At Westmere Payments, a fictional payments processor, Grace Ellery has been in settlements operations for eleven years. She trained most of the current team, and colleagues go to her when a payout does not reconcile. Her manager has noticed that she insists on handling month-end reconciliations of the merchant payout account herself and has declined offers of help. The manager mentions this to the fraud team as “a bit odd but nothing wrong”. Grace has no disciplinary history and her reconciliations have always balanced.
4.1.question: How should the fraud team treat this information?
4.1.answer: As a risk indicator that justifies a quiet, proportionate check, not as an accusation. Refusing to take leave and insisting on sole control of a process are both behaviours the ACFE reports in cases that were later discovered. Long tenure and sole control of a reconciliation also create the conditions in which a scheme can run unobserved. The fact that the reconciliation always balances is not comfort: a person who controls the reconciliation controls what it shows. The sound response is to treat it as a control question first. Arrange for another person to perform or review the reconciliation, and require continuous leave for the role, as would apply to any role with this level of control. If the process is changed for everyone in the role, no individual is singled out. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Occupational fraud is committed against the employer, and the ACFE classifies it into asset misappropriation, corruption and financial statement fraud. — Asset misappropriation splits into cash schemes (skimming, larceny, fraudulent disbursements) and non-cash schemes, including the theft of information. — Corruption covers conflicts of interest, bribery, illegal gratuities and economic extortion, and it is hard to detect because the books still balance. — Financial statement fraud is the least common branch and usually involves senior people who can override controls. — A single case often touches more than one branch, and the ACFE counts it under each. — Perpetrators are usually trusted first-time offenders, and warning signs such as refusing leave or a close vendor tie justify a check of the records, not an accusation. — The ACFE data describes fraud against employers; it is not a measure of external fraud against banks. 83

4.2.title: THE NEW SUPPLIER
4.2.situation: Larchmont Bank, a fictional regional bank, runs a quarterly analytics review of its vendor master file. The review flags Northgate Facilities Ltd, set up eight months ago. Northgate has a single address that is a residential flat, no website, and a bank account in the name of a different person. It has issued invoices every month for “facilities consultancy”, each between the department head’s approval limit and the amount that would require a second approver. All invoices were approved by Tom Whitfield, a department head, who also requested the vendor’s creation.
4.2.question: What does the pattern suggest, and what should the analyst do first?
4.2.answer: The pattern matches a shell vendor scheme: a vendor with no business footprint, a bank account that does not match the supplier name, invoices for an intangible service, values placed below the second-approval level, and the same person requesting the vendor and approving its invoices. That is a failure of segregation of duties, the very separation that is meant to prevent one person from creating and paying a supplier. Together they are strong grounds to investigate. The first step is not to stop payment in a way that tips Tom off. The analyst should preserve the records, confirm independently whether Northgate exists and whether any service was delivered, and refer the matter to the investigation function under the confidentiality rules. The analyst should preserve the records, confirm independently whether Northgate exists and whether any service was delivered, and refer the matter to the investigation function under the confidentiality rules.

4.2.title: THE THREE-WAY MATCH THAT PASSED
4.2.situation: Delmar Credit, a fictional lender, pays its facilities contractors only after a three-way match. An internal review finds that Marta Kowal, a facilities manager, has approved a series of invoices from Ashgrove Maintenance for “ongoing site inspections”. Each purchase order, service confirmation and invoice agreed, so every payment passed the match. But Marta created the purchase orders, signed the service confirmations herself because no one else was assigned to the sites, and chose Ashgrove without a tender. Ashgrove is owned by a former colleague of hers. No one has ever checked that inspections took place.
4.2.question: Why did the three-way match fail to catch this, and what should change?
4.2.answer: The match confirms that three documents agree, not that the documents are true. Here all three came from the same person, so they agreed by construction. The control was undermined by a lack of segregation of duties: the person who requested the service also confirmed that it had been delivered. In addition, the award of the contract without competition, and the personal link to the owner, are conflict-of-interest and bid-rigging indicators that the match was never designed to see. 86 The fix is to separate the roles. Someone independent of the requester should confirm delivery, for services as well as goods, by an inspection report, access log or site visit. Awards without tender should be approved by a second person, and staff should declare relationships with suppliers. The error to avoid is to conclude that the control is useless: a three-way match is valuable when the people who feed it are independent. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Expense schemes use mischaracterised, fictitious, overstated or duplicate claims, and rely on claims being approved without close checking. — Payroll fraud centres on ghost employees, falsified pay and diverted bank details, and the plainest red flag is a mismatch between people paid and people who can be shown to exist. — Shell vendor schemes show up in the vendor master file: unusual addresses, bank accounts that match employees, consecutive invoice numbers and amounts just under approval limits. — Kickbacks and bid rigging leave the books balanced and are found by comparison: price benchmarking, spend by vendor and repeat winners. — A conflict of interest that is declared and managed is a business matter, and a hidden one is a warning sign. — Three-way match, approval limits and bank-detail change controls work only when the people feeding them are independent of each other, and mandatory leave helps by exposing schemes that need daily attention. — Controls must apply to senior people too, because override of controls is a recurring weakness. 87

4.3.title: TOO MANY LOOKUPS
4.3.situation: At Larchmont Bank’s contact centre, the weekly access analytics report shows that Danielle Moreau, an agent on the cards team, opened roughly four times as many customer profiles as the average agent in her team over the past month. Most of these profiles belong to high-value customers. Her call log shows far fewer completed calls than her profile views would suggest, and about a third of the profiles she viewed have no call recorded against them. Agents on her team are entitled to open any customer profile, so nothing was blocked.
4.3.question: What should the fraud and security team conclude, and what should they do?
4.3.answer: They should conclude that the pattern is unexplained and needs investigation, not that Danielle is guilty. Profile views that do not match calls are a classic sign of browsing for a purpose other than service, which could be curiosity, data theft for sale, or lookups made for an outsider. The concentration on high-balance customers raises the concern from privacy breach to possible fraud preparation. A sound practitioner preserves the access logs, widens the check to see whether any of the viewed accounts has since had a change of contact details, new payee or takeover attempt, and escalates under the confidential insider-investigation process involving HR and legal. The practitioner does not question Danielle first, and does not rely on her supervisor’s opinion as an alibi.

4.4.title: THE BROKER WHO NEVER FAILS
4.4.situation: Delmar Credit receives personal-loan applications through a network of brokers, and many of its loans are written through them. The fraud team notices that Sundial Finance, a broker introduced a year ago, has an unusually low rate of declined applications, and that a high share of its approved loans go into early arrears with the first payment missed. Sundial is paid commission on each funded loan, and its commission rate is the highest in the network.
4.4.question: How should the fraud team read this, and what should it do?
4.4.answer: The team should read it as a probable application fraud pattern involving the broker, until the data show otherwise. Low declines with early default is the typical outcome when applications are doctored to pass the firm’s checks. The commission structure gives Sundial a reason to inflate. Passing due diligence at onboarding is a snapshot taken a year ago; it does not show how Sundial behaves now, and the absence of complaints is not evidence of quality when the victims may be the firm itself or identities whose real owners have not yet been contacted. The team should compare Sundial’s applications with those from other sources, sample the files for verification of income and employer, and share its findings with the relationship manager and the third-party risk function. Depending on the findings it may suspend new business pending review, invoke contract rights to audit and to claw back commission, and consider reporting.

4.4.title: CUTTING OFF THE CALL CENTRE
4.4.situation: Larchmont Bank outsources part of its card servicing to Larkfield Contact Services, whose staff work in a separate building and use the bank’s systems through remote logins. The fraud team’s analytics show that card replacements and address changes handled by one Larkfield team have been followed by unauthorised transactions at a much higher rate than for the bank’s own agents. The contract allows audit and termination for cause. A senior manager proposes ending the contract at once by sending notice, and removing Larkfield’s access to all systems the same day. The legal adviser suggests collecting the relevant records first.
4.4.question: What is the sound sequence?
4.4.answer: The legal adviser is right: evidence first. The bank should first secure its own logs, recordings and the data that show the pattern. It should add extra verification to the affected actions without announcing why. It should invoke its audit and cooperation rights only after legal advice, once its own evidence is secure, because invoking them tells Larkfield that the bank is looking, and Larkfield or some of its staff may be involved. If the bank gives notice and cuts access immediately, Larkfield’s records, and the opportunity to identify the individuals involved, may be lost, and the bank may find it has weakened its own position under the contract. 95 At the same time, the bank should not wait for certainty before protecting customers. It can add extra verification to the high-risk actions the Larkfield team performs, for example a second approval or a call to the customer for card replacements and address changes, presented as a general control change, and can monitor affected accounts closely. Termination, reporting and customer contact follow once the facts are clear, with legal and regulatory advice. Containment and evidence preservation can proceed together. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A third party can be a victim, a tool or a perpetrator of fraud, and in practice customers and supervisors look to the institution for what its outsourcers do in its name. — The fraud risk assessment must cover third parties, and the UK failure-to-prevent-fraud offence can reach frauds by agents and service providers only where the fraud was intended to benefit the organisation (Chapter 2.6 and Module 7). — Brokers and agents paid on volume have a built-in incentive to inflate, so their results must be tested against the firm’s own data. — Due diligence should verify ownership, record, staff vetting, controls and subcontractors, and should rely on evidence, not on self-completed questionnaires. — Contracts should secure standards, audit, prompt reporting, cooperation, control of subcontracting, remedies and data handling, and the rights must actually be used. — Monitoring should track fraud-specific indicators for each third party, not only service quality. — Exit planning should allow evidence to be preserved and access to be restricted before a suspect third party is told, and containment can proceed while termination is prepared. 96

4.5.title: THE ANONYMOUS MESSAGE
4.5.situation: Corvane Bank’s web hotline receives an anonymous message: “The head of procurement is splitting orders to stay under the tender limit, and a supplier called Ridgeway pays for his holidays.” The message gives two purchase order numbers and no name. The hotline allows anonymous replies. The compliance officer, Neil Archer, considers three options: ignore it because it is anonymous and unsupported, forward the full message to the head of procurement’s own director for comment, or log it, test the purchase orders independently and reply through the system asking for more detail.
4.5.question: Which option is sound, and why?
4.5.answer: The third. An anonymous report is still information, and the message contains specific, checkable details: two purchase order numbers, a named supplier and a described method. Order splitting and supplier hospitality are recognised bid-rigging and kickback indicators (Chapter 4.2). The bank should check the orders against the tender limit and the supplier’s history, and look for gifts or hospitality records, while keeping the circle of knowledge small. Replying through the system invites the reporter to add facts without revealing identity. Ignoring the message would waste a lead, and the ACFE’s research puts tips at the head of detection methods. Forwarding it to the director would break confidentiality, risk alerting the person concerned and may involve someone who is not independent. The right approach is to treat the report as a lead to test, not as proof, and to protect both the reporter and the person reported until facts are known.

4.5.title: A HOTLINE THAT NOBODY USES
4.5.situation: Delmar Credit reports to its audit committee that its ethics hotline, run by the human resources department, received only two reports last year, both about workplace conduct. The head of HR presents this as evidence of a strong ethical culture and proposes no change. A recent internal audit found that most staff did not know the hotline number, that reports are logged in a spreadsheet kept by HR, and that two employees who had raised concerns informally with their managers said they later felt sidelined. Internally, the fraud team has also discovered a purchasing scheme that no one had reported.
4.5.question: Is the low volume of reports reassuring?
4.5.answer: No. The surrounding facts point to a channel that is not trusted or not known. Staff do not know the number, the reports are held by a department that also handles staff discipline, and the people who spoke up say they were treated badly. A scheme was running unreported. The ACFE’s research finds that tips are the leading way in which fraud is detected, so a near-absence of tips alongside an undetected scheme suggests that the channel is not doing its job. A low count measures use, not the level of honesty. A sound practitioner would recommend a review of the channel: publicise it with a route that bypasses HR and management, such as an independent provider or the audit committee, secure the case log, check how the two informal reporters were treated, state that retaliation is misconduct, and report to the committee on use, speed, outcomes and staff awareness. 99 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Tips are the most common single route by which the ACFE finds occupational fraud to have been detected, and employees are the largest source. — A good reporting system offers several channels, including one that bypasses management, and is open to customers, vendors and agents as well as staff. — Anonymity, confidentiality and non-retaliation are different protections, and a programme should offer all three and be honest about their limits. — Whistleblower protection laws exist in many jurisdictions, but the specific rules are outside this guide, and an internal policy should not depend on the reporter knowing them. — Handling a report means recording it, triaging it by an independent and trained person, investigating with an open mind, giving feedback and learning from the result. — ACFE guidance on professional investigations expects evidence to be controlled, confidentiality to be kept, and no opinion to be given on legal guilt. — A hotline is judged by trust, speed and outcomes, and a low report count may signal distrust, not a clean organisation. 100 MODULE 5 Detection and analytics Prevention stops what it can see coming, and detection catches the rest. This module shows how a financial institution decides what to look for, where to look, and what to do when something looks wrong. It covers detection strategy, red flags and rules, statistical and machine-learning models, the management of alerts, authentication and device signals, and the governance that keeps all of it honest. The mechanics of scoring, velocity checks, behavioural signals and alert tuning are practitioner method and differ from firm to firm. Where a standard or official alert applies, the module describes its principles and states its limits, and the legal frame is in Module 7. 101

5.1.title: THE OVERNIGHT FILE
5.1.situation: Harrow Mutual, a regional bank, offers instant account-to-account transfers through its mobile app. Its fraud team runs a detailed monitoring job every night that joins payment, device, login and complaint data and is accurate at spotting accounts that receive money from several unrelated senders. For months the nightly alerts have identified mule accounts, but the money has always left those accounts by the time the analyst opens the case. The head of fraud proposes to buy a second, more sophisticated nightly tool to improve accuracy.
5.1.question: Is a more accurate nightly tool the right response?
5.1.answer: No. The weakness is timing, not accuracy. The nightly job already identifies the right accounts. It identifies them after the funds have gone, because instant transfers settle in seconds and cannot easily be pulled back. A second batch tool would find the same accounts equally late. A sound practitioner would take what the batch job learns and push it into the real-time path. For example, accounts flagged as likely mules can go onto a watch list that the payment flow checks at once, so that money arriving into or leaving them is held or reviewed. Another option is a near-real-time rule that looks for a burst of unrelated inbound payments followed by rapid outbound movement. The batch job stays, but as the source of intelligence, not the control.

5.1.title: THE THREE QUIET SYSTEMS
5.1.situation: At Tessel Credit Union, a member’s phone number is changed through the call centre on Monday. On Tuesday the member’s online banking is accessed from a device never seen before. On Wednesday, a payment much larger than the member’s usual goes to a new payee. The call-centre system, the digital-banking system and the payments system each hold one of these events. Each system has its own rules, and each event on its own was below that system’s alert level. The member lost the funds. The fraud manager says the rules in each system worked as designed and the loss was unlucky.
5.1.question: Is that a fair conclusion?
5.1.answer: No. Each rule worked as designed, but the design left a gap between systems. The three events are the classic sequence of an account takeover: contact details changed, a new device, then an out-of-pattern payment. No single system could see the sequence because none held all three events, so the strategy had no point at which the combined pattern could be detected. The fix is to build coverage for the typology, not for the system. That means feeding the three event types into one place where a rule or model can look for the sequence within a short time window, and agreeing what action follows, such as a hold on the payment and a call to the member on the previously registered number. Calling it unlucky hides a design flaw that will repeat. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Detection can happen at application, login, payment set-up, in flight, after release and in look-back, and the earlier moments leave more choices. — Real-time, near-real-time and batch detection suit different jobs, and batch alone is a late warning for payments that cannot be recalled. — A strategy needs an action ladder from silent flag to block, with friction weighed against the cost of a missed fraud. — Intelligence found in batch analysis should be pushed into the real-time path, for example through watch lists. — Coverage is tested with a matrix of typologies against detection moments, and empty cells show where nothing is watching. — Fraud signals sit in separate systems, so a strategy needs a shared view that can see sequences across them. 104

5.2.title: THE NEW PAYEE RULE
5.2.situation: Wexmoor Bank has a rule that holds any outbound payment above a set amount to a payee added in the last 24 hours. Nearly all alerts turn out to be genuine: customers paying builders, landlords and online sellers. A product manager proposes switching the rule off because it causes friction without catching much. The fraud analyst, Daniel Okoro, looks at the cases that were fraud over the past quarter and finds that almost all had a second feature in common: the login came from a device the bank had not seen before. Among the genuine payments the rule held, very few came from a new device, because honest customers usually pay from the phone they always use.
5.2.question: What should Daniel recommend?
5.2.answer: He should recommend keeping the signal but changing the rule. A new payee on its own is a weak signal that most honest customers also produce. A new payee combined with a new device is far rarer among honest customers and far more common in the confirmed frauds he found. Turning the rule into a compound condition keeps its power to catch takeover fraud while cutting the volume of alerts on ordinary payments. The tempting error is to treat a noisy rule as a bad rule. Often the signal is sound and the condition is too loose. Before changing it, Daniel should test the new version against past data, including genuine payments, to see how many frauds it would still catch and how many alerts it would remove.

5.2.title: THE RULE NOBODY OWNS
5.2.situation: During a review, Mira Castellan, a fraud strategy manager at Larchmont Bank, finds hundreds of active detection rules. For a quarter of them no owner is recorded, and for many the original reason is not documented. Several generate alerts every week, and analysts close nearly all of them as genuine without comment. A colleague suggests deleting every ownerless rule that produces no confirmed fraud, to cut the queue quickly. Mira notes that two of the ownerless rules were added shortly after a large loss, though nobody on the current team was there at the time.
5.2.question: Is deleting them at once the right approach?
5.2.answer: Not at once. A rule that finds no confirmed fraud may be useless, but it may also be doing its job as a deterrent or as cover for a rare, severe scheme. Without an owner or a stated purpose, nobody can judge which. Deleting on the basis of alert history alone risks removing the only control for an uncommon but costly typology. A sound approach is to find an owner for each rule, document its purpose, then test it against past data. Rules that are redundant or have no supporting rationale are retired through the normal change process, with a record of the decision. Where a rule is doubtful but cannot be tested yet, it can run in monitor-only mode, producing no customer impact, while evidence is gathered. This reduces the queue without creating blind spots. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A red flag is a reason to look closer, not proof, and its meaning depends on context. — Combinations of independent signals are far more informative than any single signal. — A rule has conditions, parameters, an action and an owner, and rules come in static, list-based, comparison and sequence families. — A velocity check counts events or value over a time period and is usually set by customer segment. — Rules are fast and explainable but lag behind new schemes and tend to accumulate without being retired. — Every rule needs an owner, a documented purpose, tested parameters and a review date. 107

5.3.title: THE FLAT HISTOGRAM
5.3.situation: An internal auditor at Brannock Group runs a Benford-type test on expense claims across five hundred employees and finds that one department’s claims depart noticeably from the expected leading-digit pattern. A colleague suggests escalating the department head to the investigations team as a suspected fraudster. The auditor notes that the expense policy requires manager approval above a fixed amount, and that many claims in the flagged department fall just under it. Other departments with the same policy show a smaller but similar clustering.
5.3.question: What does the test result support?
5.3.answer: It supports a closer look at the department’s claims, not an accusation. A policy cap or approval threshold shapes amounts and creates a departure from the natural pattern with no dishonesty involved, since many people simply claim up to the limit. The Benford-type test is known to be unreliable where thresholds distort the figures, so the departure here has an innocent explanation that must be ruled out first. That said, a cluster of claims just under an approval limit is worth reviewing in its own right, since it can also indicate someone avoiding review. The auditor should examine the receipts and claim patterns, compare them with similar departments, and keep the review factual. 109

5.4.title: THE BETTER-LOOKING RULE
5.4.situation: At Oakridge Bank, a manager reviews two versions of a card rule. Version one raises 8,000 alerts a month and catches 400 frauds. Version two raises 2,500 alerts and catches 250 frauds. The manager, Helen Marsh, notes that version two has much higher precision and wants to adopt it because the analyst team is overloaded. Finance gives her two planning figures: a review costs about 5 currency units of analyst time, and the average card fraud that gets through costs about 400 units.
5.4.question: On these figures, which version is cheaper, and what method should Helen use to decide?
5.4.answer: Version one is cheaper, and Helen should compare total cost, not precision alone. Version two removes 5,500 alerts, which saves 27,500 units of review time. But it catches 150 fewer frauds a month, and 150 times 400 is 60,000 units of loss. Version two therefore costs about 32,500 units more each month before customer friction is counted. The method is to set the review time saved against the losses added, using the review cost per alert, the average loss per fraud and ideally some measure of customer friction. There is also a middle route. Helen could keep version one’s coverage but sort the alerts by risk, so that the highest-scoring get a full review and the lowest get a faster, lighter check or an automated customer message. This keeps recall while easing the load. The error to avoid is optimising the metric that is easiest to improve.

5.4.title: WHAT SHOULD HAVE HAPPENED ON MONDAY
5.4.situation: Return to Halvern Savings. On the Monday, the strategy analyst has found that the new-payee rule is the largest source of alerts and wants to reduce them. Susan Achterberg asks her team what the right first step is before any threshold is changed. Three suggestions are made. The first is to raise the threshold now and monitor the queue. The second is to run the proposed new settings in monitor-only mode alongside the live rule and compare what each would have caught on the past month’s data. The third is to switch the rule off for a week and see what happens.
5.4.question: Which is the sound first step, and why?
5.4.answer: The second. Running the proposed settings in monitor-only mode, and testing them against past confirmed fraud, shows how many frauds the new version would have missed before any customer is exposed. It costs a little time and no risk. The change can then be approved on evidence, with an independent reviewer, and released with a planned check afterwards. 113 The first option changes a live control on the evidence of a shorter queue, which is the mistake that led to the loss. A sound practitioner also asks whether the queue can be eased in other ways while the analysis runs, such as sorting by risk or automating customer confirmation of low-risk payments. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Alerts form a funnel, and a team should measure every step, with a sudden jump in alert volume treated as a signal to investigate. — Precision is the share of alerts that were real fraud, recall is the share of real fraud that was alerted, and overall accuracy misleads because fraud is rare. — Loosening a threshold raises recall and lowers precision, and the right setting balances missed-fraud losses against review cost and customer friction. — False positives cost analyst time and customer trust, and the aim is fewer unnecessary ones, not none. — Good queues are prioritised, segmented and timed, and closure codes feed evidence back to rule owners and model teams. — Tuning is a control change and needs a reason, a test on past data, independent approval, rollback and a check afterwards. 114

5.5.title: THE PAYMENT MADE ON THE PHONE
5.5.situation: Anya Petrova, a long-standing customer of Lindenfield Bank, logs into her app from her usual phone with correct credentials. Over twelve minutes she adds a new payee and sets up a large payment. The session shows long pauses, repeated switching between the app and another application, and slow, careful typing of the payee’s details. Her usual sessions last under two minutes. The payment is not out of range for her account, and the payee does not match any known mule or fraud list. A rule based on device and credentials passes it as low risk.
5.5.question: Which response is sound: pass the payment as low risk, block it, or add friction in proportion to the signal?
5.5.answer: Add friction in proportion to the signal. The session behaviour is an illustrative signal of a possible authorised push payment scam, even though device and credentials are genuine. Anya is the person at the keyboard, so authentication cannot help, and the session is the only clue. A long session, switching to another application (possibly a call) and careful dictation-like typing are the kind of signs some firms treat as guidance by a third party. Because the signal is weak and its reliability is not established here, the response is an informative warning screen about the scam pattern, a short delay, or a call from the bank before release. There are two errors. The tempting one is to pass the payment because the device and login are good. The other is to block it outright: behavioural signals indicate risk without proving it, and the payment may be entirely hers. The action ladder from Chapter 5.1 fits: add friction that gives a genuine customer room to think and the bank a chance to ask questions, while letting a payment that is truly hers go ahead.

5.5.title: THE CAMERA THAT WOULD NOT COOPERATE
5.5.situation: Orchard Digital, an online lender, runs live video checks for new applicants. An applicant, “Lukas Brandt”, is asked to turn his head, but the video lags and freezes. He says his camera is faulty and asks to switch to a different application on his phone for the call. The identity document photo looks slightly smoother than usual around the edges, and his phone number and email were created recently. A supervisor has reminded the team that approvals are slow this week and applicants are dropping out, and the agent wonders whether to approve because the document data matches the application form.
5.5.question: Which action is sound: approve because the document data matches, accuse the applicant of fraud, or decline to proceed on this session and use another verification route?
5.5.answer: The third. The agent should treat this as a cluster of signals consistent with a possible injection or deepfake attempt, and should not approve on document data alone. Document data matching the form means little, because the information on a synthetic or stolen identity is internally consistent by design. The red flags are the freeze when asked to move, the request to change channel, the unusual photo quality and the recently created contact details. The FinCEN alert lists switching channels and technical glitches during live checks among its red flags. 117 Accusation is also wrong: no single flag proves fraud, as the alert itself cautions. The sound step is not to accuse the applicant but to decline to proceed on this session and require another verification route, such as a fresh live session in the lender’s own channel, further document checks or a higher-assurance method. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Authentication proves identity, assurance is the confidence in the result, and the NIST digital identity guidelines grade authentication into levels of assurance. — Phishing-resistant authenticators resist being handed over to a criminal, which is why codes alone do not stop account takeover, while authorised scams are a different problem because the customer is the one authenticating. — Fraud signals such as location or device inform the risk decision but do not raise the authentication assurance level. — Device intelligence asks whether a device is new, shared, emulated or tied to earlier fraud, and it is one input and not a verdict. — Behavioural signals are used by some firms to suggest a different person at the keyboard or a customer being guided, their reliability is not established here, and they justify friction and not blocking on their own. — Consortium data finds criminals who move between institutions, but a shared hit must be verified and the sharing rules are in Chapter 6.5 and Module 7. — The FinCEN deepfake alert lists red flags such as webcam plug-ins and channel switching, and warns that red flags need context. 118

5.6.title: THE POSTCODE THAT PREDICTS
5.6.situation: Fieldgate Bank’s new card-fraud model includes a feature that groups customers by neighbourhood, based on historic confirmed fraud in each area. The model’s overall performance is strong. A fairness review by analyst Imogen Rhys finds that customers in two particular neighbourhoods are three times as likely to have a card declined, even though a sample review finds most of those declines were genuine purchases. The modelling lead argues that the feature is predictive and the results only reflect real risk. No one has yet compared error rates between neighbourhoods.
5.6.question: What should the review conclude?
5.6.answer: The strong overall performance does not answer the fairness question. The feature carries past investigation patterns: areas where more fraud was confirmed in the past, perhaps because more attention was paid to them, are scored as riskier, and so customers who live there face more declines of genuine purchases. If the neighbourhoods are also linked to a protected characteristic, the feature may act as a proxy for it. The sample review, which found mostly genuine declines, suggests the feature is producing errors that fall on certain customers. The sound response is to test the model with and without the feature, compare error rates by group, and consider replacing the area-based feature with behavioural features that describe the customer’s own activity. The decision and its reasons should be documented, and escalated through the model governance route. Predictive power alone is not a defence when the cost of errors is unevenly shared.

5.6.title: THE FEED THAT WENT QUIET
5.6.situation: Marlow Card Services runs a machine-learning fraud model that depends partly on a feed of device data from a third-party provider. After a supplier update, one field in that feed, indicating whether a device is new, starts arriving blank for many events. Nobody changes the model. Over the next three weeks the model’s alert rate falls steadily and the fraud team celebrates fewer alerts. The head of model validation, Kwame Asante, notices that fraud losses reported by customers are rising at the same time.
5.6.question: What has happened, and what should Kwame recommend?
5.6.answer: The silent change in the data feed has altered the model’s inputs. Because the new-device field is blank, the model cannot see a key signal, so it scores risky events as lower risk. The fall in alerts is not good news; it reflects blindness, and rising customer-reported losses point the same way. This is a data-quality failure that model monitoring should have caught through input-stability checks. Kwame should recommend restoring the field with the supplier, or reverting to a state in which the model can run correctly, at once. A review of events since the change should follow, to find frauds that slipped through. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — US model risk guidance is supervisory, not statute, expects an inventory, validation, monitoring and ownership scaled to materiality, and treats generative and agentic AI as outside its scope. — An exclusion from model guidance is not an exclusion from risk management, and the wider legal frame is in Module 7. — Validation covers conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis and ongoing monitoring, and it should be independent of the model builders. — Explainability, the ability to say why a model produced a score, matters for analysts, customers and auditors, and a model whose reasons cannot be given plainly is hard to govern. — Fairness testing compares alert, decline and error rates across groups, and predictive power does not excuse errors that fall unevenly. — Data quality failures can change scores without anyone touching the model, so inputs need monitoring. — Change control requires a reason, testing, approval, versioning and rollback, and human review must be informed and not a formality. 121 MODULE 6 Investigation and response Detection tells an institution that something may be wrong. This module covers what happens next: turning an alert into a case, investigating it fairly, treating the customer properly, trying to get money back, reporting to the right people, and learning from the outcome. Case triage, interview technique and recovery processes differ between firms, so those parts are taught as practitioner method and labelled as such. Where an authoritative source exists, the module uses it directly: the ACFE Code of Professional Standards, a professional code for examiners that this guide uses as a reference for good practice and not as a rule that binds bank staff; the Cifas filing standard; and the principles of suspicious activity reporting. 122

6.1.title: THE ALERT THAT LOOKED SMALL
6.1.situation: At Larchmont Bank, first-line analyst Tomasz Reid reviews a queue of alerts. One is a new payee added to a retail account followed by a modest transfer, still marked pending. The customer, Mrs Adaeze Okafor, called the branch twice last week confused about a text message, and a note on her profile records both calls. The system ranks the alert low because of the amount. Tomasz notices that the same payee was added to two other accounts earlier that morning. Another analyst suggests clearing the queue in amount order and returning to the pattern after lunch.
6.1.question: How should Tomasz triage the alert?
6.1.answer: He should treat it as urgent. A pending payment means money may still be stoppable, the profile note suggests the customer may be vulnerable, and the same beneficiary on three accounts is a pattern. Funds in motion, recoverability, victim and pattern all raise priority; only the amount points the other way. The sound steps are to hold the pending payment under procedure, contact Mrs Okafor through a verified channel, open a case linking the three accounts, and ask whether the payee account can be restricted or reported, noting the time of each step.

6.1.title: THE THEORY THAT FITTED TOO WELL
6.1.situation: Hannah Ellery, an investigator at Delmar Credit, opens a case on a card account after a series of overseas purchases the customer says he did not make. Her first theory is cloned card data, and she begins pulling merchant records. She then sees that each purchase was approved in the banking app from the family tablet, which the customer registered as a trusted device long ago and which his teenage son began using the week before the purchases started. The approvals came at times when the customer says he was at work. She decides the approvals are probably a system quirk and leaves them out of her notes so the file stays tidy.
6.1.question: What has gone wrong with Hannah’s approach, and what should she do?
6.1.answer: Hannah has let an early theory decide which facts count. The app approvals from the registered tablet point away from card cloning, and tablet access is an explanation she has not tested. The Code’s requirement to weigh evidence that cuts against the leading theory (IV.A.3) means the approvals belong in the file, marked as unexplained. Leaving them out also makes the record misleading to the next reader. She should restate the case with two explanations, cloned data and use of a trusted device by someone with access, decide what would separate them (the timing of each approval against the tablet’s device log and who held the tablet), and record the change of scope. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — An alert is a signal, a referral is a person’s concern, a case is a record opened for real investigation, and a disposition is the recorded outcome. — Triage asks about harm first: is money in motion, can it be stopped, who is the victim, is anyone vulnerable, is an insider involved and is there a pattern. — A case record needs an owner, a type, timestamps, linked cases and enough detail that a colleague can pick it up cold. — Set predication and scope at the start and reassess them as evidence arrives, as the ACFE Code of Professional Standards asks. — Weigh evidence that points away from the leading theory, and record it even when it makes the file untidy. 125

6.2.title: THE EMPLOYEE INTERVIEW
6.2.situation: Larchmont Bank’s investigations team is looking at a branch employee, Dmitri Volkov, who accessed several dormant accounts that were then used for outgoing payments. Lead investigator Ines Carvalho wants to interview him that afternoon. A colleague suggests she call it a routine records check, hoping he will speak more freely, and then press him on the access log if he is vague. HR has not been told, the bank has not decided whether to refer the matter to the police, and Dmitri does not know he is under review.
6.2.question: Is the colleague’s approach sound, and what should Ines do first?
6.2.answer: It is not sound. Describing a suspected-misconduct interview as a routine check is deceptive, and pressing a person on a log to extract an admission aims at a confession, not information. Both break the fairness principle: an interview seeks information and tells the truth about its purpose. A statement obtained that way may be unreliable and may harm later disciplinary or criminal steps. Ines should pause and speak to HR and legal counsel about local rights, whether he may be accompanied, and whether the police should be involved first. If an interview goes ahead, she plans it, explains its purpose truthfully, asks open questions, records it at the time and stops if he asks for representation, while preserving the access logs.

6.2.title: THE REPORT THAT WENT TOO FAR
6.2.situation: Rafael Montes, an analyst at Delmar Credit, finishes a report on a suspected application fraud. The evidence shows that the identity documents were submitted from a device linked to three other applications, that the phone number was registered the same week, and that the applicant has not responded to two requests for a call. His draft says: “The applicant is a fraudster who fabricated his identity and should be prosecuted.” His manager asks him to add a paragraph on the documents that were consistent with a genuine applicant, which Rafael had left out as not helpful.
6.2.question: What is wrong with the draft, and how should it be corrected?
6.2.answer: The draft expresses an opinion on legal guilt, which the Code says a report must not do (V.B.2), and it leaves out evidence that points the other way, against the duty to weigh evidence on both sides (IV.A.3). A report that omits it risks being misleading (V.A.1). The facts stated are enough to support a referral without characterisation, which adds nothing and exposes the institution if the explanation proves innocent. A corrected report states the shared device, the phone number timing and the non-response as findings, with sources, and includes the consistent documents with a note of what they do and do not establish. It lists what is unresolved, such as whether the applicant’s identity can be verified by another route, and it recommends the next steps. The decision to refer or prosecute belongs to the people with authority to make it, not to the analyst’s wording. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — An examination should be legal, professional and thorough, and seek evidence that is complete, reliable and relevant. — Chain of custody records who held evidence and what was done to it, and digital evidence should be preserved before it is analysed. — A timeline separates facts from inferences, notes time zones and shows gaps; a link between accounts is a lead and not a conclusion. — Interviewing is planned, open, fair and documented at the time; it never uses deception, threats or pressure, and employee interviews need HR and legal advice first. — A report rests on sufficient, reliable and relevant evidence, is not misleading, and gives no opinion on legal guilt or innocence. 128

6.3.title: THE CUSTOMER WITH A SCRIPT
6.3.situation: Delmar Credit’s fraud team calls Mr Gerald Whitcombe, aged eighty-one, about a large transfer to a new payee. He says the payment is fine and the payee is a government officer who is helping him with a tax matter. He sounds anxious and says he has been told not to discuss it with the bank, and a second voice can be heard giving instructions. The agent’s script says to confirm consent and release the payment if consent is given.
6.3.question: What should the agent do?
6.3.answer: The agent should not simply release the payment on the strength of consent. Mr Whitcombe’s age is not the reason. The signs are those of a coached victim of an impersonation scam: a story about officials, an instruction not to speak to the bank, urgency and a prompting voice. Consent given under that influence may not be his own. The script is a guide, and the situation calls for the scam-intervention procedure, at a calm pace and with care for his dignity. The agent should hold the payment briefly, for only as long as the checks need, and escalate the same day to a senior colleague who can decide within the account terms and the law (Module 7), avoiding accusation: “Many people have been contacted by someone pretending to be an official, and we want to be certain this is safe.” Offer to call him back on a number he knows, and consider contacting a trusted person with his consent.

6.3.title: THE HOLD NOBODY REVIEWED
6.3.situation: Larchmont Bank places a hold on the account of a small business owner, Sofia Duarte, after an alert on several incoming payments. The case owner moves to another team and the case is not reassigned. Eleven days later Sofia calls, unable to pay her suppliers. The agent sees only a restriction code and “under review”, and is tempted to say it is routine and will be lifted soon.
6.3.question: What should the agent do, and what does the case show about the process?
6.3.answer: The agent should not promise a lifting date that nobody has set. The sound response is to apologise for the lack of contact, say truthfully what can be said, escalate immediately to find the owner or reassign the case, and agree a time by which she will be called back, logging the contact and the complaint. The agent should not speculate about the reason or the outcome. The process failure is that a hold had no owner, no review date and no communication plan. Every hold needs all three. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — First contact uses a verified channel, never asks for credentials or passcodes, states what was seen in neutral words and starts with an open question. — Vulnerability is a state, not a label, and signs such as confusion, urgency or a prompting voice are reasons to slow down and adapt, not proof of anything. — A customer’s consent given under coaching or pressure may not be their own, so a suspicious payment is held only briefly and the decision is escalated. — Every hold needs an owner, a review date and a communication plan, and the customer should be told what is happening in plain words. — Explain decisions with the outcome, the main reason, the next step and the route to complain, without disclosing detection rules or confidential reports. — Complaints are data about the process; claims are decided on written, consistent criteria and a claim is tested against the evidence and never assumed to be false. 131

6.4.title: THE DISPUTE AND THE LABEL
6.4.situation: Delmar Credit’s cardholder, Aisha Rahman, disputes a purchase from an online electronics seller, saying she did not make it. The issuer’s dispute team has the authentication record, which shows a successful step-up check on her registered phone, and a delivery record to her home address. The team lead wants to reject the dispute and mark Aisha a probable first-party fraudster. A colleague suggests first checking who else has access to her phone or receives parcels at that address. Aisha says she was at work.
6.4.question: Can the team label Aisha a first-party fraudster on this evidence, and what should it do first?
6.4.answer: No, and the colleague’s approach is the sound one. The authentication and delivery records weigh against an unauthorised-transaction claim, but they do not show who held the phone or who received the parcel. Moving straight to a label of first-party fraud skips the step of testing the explanation, and a wrong label can harm the customer and expose the institution to a complaint. The first step is to put the evidence to Aisha and ask about access to her phone and the delivery address. What follows depends on her answer. If a household member made the purchase, it is a customer conversation, not a fraud finding.
