If she cannot account for the records, the institution decides on the evidence, records its reasons and explains the outcome and her right to complain, with no label beyond what the evidence supports. 133 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Recovery depends on speed: act in minutes, not in batches, and keep out-of-hours contacts that work. — A recall is a request to the receiving institution; a freeze is that institution’s own action, so the quality of the alert decides how it is treated. — A chargeback turns on the right dispute reason and on evidence such as authentication and delivery records. — Insurance, restitution and civil recovery are slower routes with conditions and limits; insurers expect prompt notice and preserved evidence. — Law enforcement can compel evidence and seize assets, so report early with a clear package and respond to formal requests through one team. 134

6.5.title: THE CUSTOMER WHO ASKED DIRECTLY
6.5.situation: Larchmont Bank has restricted the account of Mr Pavel Novak, whose account received several scam payments from different people in a single week. The compliance function has told the fraud team that it is dealing with the matter and has instructed staff not to discuss the case with the customer. Mr Novak telephones the branch, angry that his card no longer works. An agent tempted to calm him says, “Don’t worry, it is just paperwork”; another suggests saying nothing has been reported. Mr Novak asks directly: “Have you reported me to anyone?”
6.5.question: What should the agent say?
6.5.answer: Neither suggestion is sound. A report and its existence are confidential, so the agent should not confirm or hint that a report has been made. Saying that nothing has been reported would be false, and a false statement damages the bank’s credibility and could mislead the customer. The agent should follow the compliance function’s instruction on what may be said. 136 A sound answer describes the outcome and the next step without the mechanism: “The account is restricted while we check some recent activity. I cannot discuss the details of our checks, but I will make sure the right team knows you called and that someone contacts you by a set time.” The agent refers the call to compliance and records the contact without speculation.

6.6.title: THE ACTION THAT WAS NEVER OWNED
6.6.situation: After a similar post-incident review at Delmar Credit, a working group agrees three actions. The minutes read: “Consider improving weekend cover; rewrite the payee warning; look at linking notes.” No owners or dates are recorded, because the chair says the team knows what to do. Four months later a similar case occurs on a Saturday; the analyst escalated as required, but the duty manager also had no authority to hold, and there was no on-call route to anyone who did. The new review finds that none of the three actions has been done and that nobody remembers who was meant to act. The chair says the root cause was the weekend analyst.
6.6.question: What is wrong with the way the lessons were recorded, and with the chair’s conclusion?
6.6.answer: The actions were vague and had no owner, date or check, so nothing happened. The chair’s conclusion ends the analysis at a person, which is the human-error trap. The analyst did escalate. The root cause is that nobody on duty at the weekend had the authority or route to place a hold, a known gap from the first review. Recurrence is a sign that the earlier action was too weak or never took place, and the lessons-learned record should have made that visible. The sound response is to record each action with a named owner, due date, definition of done and follow-up check, and to track overdue items to the risk committee. The new review should treat the earlier failure to deliver as a contributing factor.

6.6.title: HINDSIGHT AT THE REVIEW TABLE
6.6.situation: At Delmar Credit, a post-incident review looks at a mule-network case that ran for six weeks before detection. A senior manager says the signs were obvious from the first week and proposes naming the two analysts who closed the early alerts as false positives. An analyst points out that the rules had been tuned shortly before to cut false positives, and that the early alerts carried none of the context that later became clear. Both analysts followed the procedure as written.
6.6.question: How should the review handle the proposal?
6.6.answer: It should decline to name individuals at this stage and judge the early decisions by what the analysts knew then. The manager is applying hindsight: the pattern is obvious once the whole story is known. The tuning decision is a contributing factor in its own right, because tuning done for a sound reason reduced sensitivity to this pattern, and it belongs in the control findings. 140 The review should ask what an analyst would have needed in week one, whether a linked-account view or aggregation rule would have supplied it, and what monitoring existed to detect lost sensitivity after tuning. Bad faith or ignoring a clear instruction goes to the proper process separately. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A post-incident review looks at systems and decisions first; blameless does not mean unaccountable, and misconduct goes to the proper process. — A root cause is the underlying reason the event was possible, found by asking why until the answer is something the institution can change. — Human error is a finding to explain, not a root cause, and hindsight makes past decisions look clearer than they were. — Findings must reach controls, the risk assessment, rules and training, each with an owner, a date and a later check. — A lessons-learned record has a fixed form, restricted access and a search route, so that patterns across cases become visible. 141 MODULE 7 Regulation, liability and technology Fraud losses raise two questions: who was cheated, and who pays. Rules on reimbursement, authentication and corporate liability decide whether a loss stays with the customer, moves to the sending firm, is shared with the receiving firm, or reaches a platform or telecommunications provider. This module teaches those rules as principles for the UK, the EU and the United States, covers Singapore, Australia and India more briefly, compares the regimes, examines AI-enabled fraud, and ends by assembling a fraud programme from Modules 1 to 6. It gives no amounts, caps or deadlines, because those change; it teaches the logic, so that a reader can read any current rule. 142

7.1.title: THE BANK THAT WANTED TO WAIT
7.1.situation: Priya Nair reports to Larchmont Bank that she paid a large sum by Faster Payments to a fraudster posing as her building contractor. She is an individual, not vulnerable, and reports within days. The money went to an account at Delmar Credit. A Larchmont analyst proposes holding the claim until Delmar Credit confirms it will pay its share, to avoid carrying the whole loss. The team lead notes that the decision clock keeps running.
7.1.question: Is the plan to wait for Delmar Credit’s confirmation compatible with the scheme?
7.1.answer: No. The sending PSP reimburses first and claims from the receiving PSP afterwards, so Larchmont’s duty does not depend on Delmar Credit agreeing to pay. The clock can be paused only for listed reasons, and waiting for the other bank’s promise is not one of them. A sound practitioner decides within the period, pays, claims the receiving firm’s share, and records any lawful pause with its reason. The tempting error is to treat the receiving bank as a guarantor whose agreement must come first.

7.1.title: THE AGENT AND THE ACCOUNTS
7.1.situation: Kestrel Lending is a single company that exceeds the limits on turnover and balance sheet total for a large organisation, although its employee count is below the limit. A broker, Daniel Ruiz, is paid for each completed loan. He falsifies income documents so that loans complete, knowing Kestrel Lending earns a fee on each. Separately, a clerk makes false expense claims. The compliance lead says neither event can engage the offence, because Kestrel Lending was not “the fraudster” and, with few employees, is not large anyway.
7.1.question: Does either event engage the offence, and is Kestrel Lending large?
7.1.answer: Only the broker’s conduct engages it. Kestrel Lending meets two of the three size tests, so it is large despite its headcount. Daniel is an agent and so can be an associated person, and he committed a fraud intending to benefit Kestrel Lending through the fees. The clerk does not engage the offence: he intends to benefit himself, and the company is the victim. The compliance lead made two errors. “Not the fraudster” misreads the offence: it is enough that the organisation failed to prevent a benefiting fraud by someone acting for it. And headcount is only one of three tests, of which two must be met. Kestrel Lending’s defence is reasonable prevention procedures, so a sound response tests the broker channel against the six principles. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The first triage question is who initiated the payment: authorised payments fall within the APP scheme, and payments made by someone else without consent are unauthorised and follow different law. — The APP scheme protects individuals, microenterprises and charities on covered systems: the sending firm reimburses first, then claims a share from the receiving firm. — A firm may refuse only for first-party fraud or gross negligence, a significant degree of carelessness, the burden of proof is the firm’s, and neither exception applies to a vulnerable customer. — Failure to prevent fraud is a corporate offence, not a reimbursement rule: a large organisation is liable for an associated person’s fraud intended to benefit it unless it shows reasonable prevention procedures. — There is no offence where the organisation was the intended victim, and an agent or service provider can be an associated person. 145

7.2.title: THE FAKE LOGIN PAGE
7.2.situation: Alder Bank, in a euro-area member state, gets a call from Marta Kowal. She entered her login details and a one-time code on a page that looked like the bank’s and then found a transfer she did not make. She calls the same day. An Alder analyst notes that the logs show a correct one-time code, concludes Marta was careless, and wants to pause the refund to investigate her conduct. No one suspects fraud.
7.2.question: Is pausing the refund consistent with the Court’s ruling as described?
7.2.answer: No. Marta reported without undue delay and nothing suggests she acted fraudulently. The PSP must refund immediately, and a belief in gross negligence does not justify holding the money back. Only a reasonable suspicion of customer fraud, reported to the authority, would. Alder should refund promptly. If it later holds evidence of intent or gross negligence, it may seek recovery from Marta, with the burden of proof on Alder. The correct code is evidence for that later question, not a reason to delay now.

7.2.title: THE POLICY THAT QUOTED A PROPOSAL
7.2.situation: Brightwater Payments has a draft customer policy: “If a scammer impersonates our staff, we will refund you in full.” The author, Luca Ferrante, who works in the compliance team of a firm serving several euro-area states, bases it on a recital in the proposed Payment Services Regulation. His manager asks whether it is accurate today. Luca says the text has been politically agreed, so it is effectively law, and proposes to launch the policy and build a refund process around it.
7.2.question: Is Luca’s reasoning sound?
7.2.answer: No. The package is proposed, not adopted. The agreed text was read only at recital level, so the operative article, the scope of “impersonation” and conditions such as police reporting are unconfirmed. A policy promising a legal right on this basis misstates the law. Brightwater can still plan: track the legislative stage, map the evidence and operations a spoofing refund would need, and treat any voluntary refund policy as a separate commercial decision made through governance. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Under PSD2 the PSP bears the burden of proof on authentication and gross negligence, and SCA with dynamic linking of amount and payee is the hinge of its liability model. — The Court’s ruling, as summarised, requires refund first for a reported unauthorised transaction, with delay only for reasonable suspicion of customer fraud and later recovery only on proof of intent or gross negligence. — A no-match name check does not block a payment, and a PSP that gives a correct result is not liable under the identifier rule if the payer proceeds. — Authorised payments to a fraudster are generally not refundable under PSD2, which is why the name check exists. — The proposed directive and Payment Services Regulation are not law until adopted, and recital-level reading must not be presented to customers as a right. 148

7.3.title: THE CLOCK STARTS AT DETECTION
7.3.situation: An analyst at Larchmont Bank reviews ACH credits into a customer account, well above the reporting threshold in total. The analyst records that the credits show clear signs of a payroll-diversion scheme and appear to be illegally derived. No suspect is identified. A senior investigator reviews the case weeks later, and a colleague formally decides a SAR is warranted later still. The team lead says the clock began on the date of that formal decision.
7.3.question: When did the filing clock start, and what follows from the team lead’s view?
7.3.answer: The clock runs from initial detection of facts that may constitute a basis for filing, not from the decision date, so it started when the analyst recorded the facts. With no suspect identified, the bank may take a limited extra period, but within an overall limit running from initial detection. Measuring from the formal decision would make the filing late. Record the date of initial detection in the case record, and do not let cases wait unobserved. Where activity is ongoing and urgent, also contact law enforcement.

7.3.title: THE FRAUD-ONLY REQUEST
7.3.situation: Noor Ahmed, an investigator at Cedar Bank, has a customer who sent a large sum to an account at Birchwood Bank after a romance-scam approach. Cedar suspects fraud only. Noor wants to ask Birchwood about the beneficiary account. Cedar’s compliance officer says the sharing route covers only money laundering, that Birchwood’s customer is not Cedar’s customer, so the route is unavailable, and that Noor should instead send Birchwood a copy of Cedar’s SAR. Both banks are assumed to be registered participants.
7.3.question: Is the compliance officer right?
7.3.answer: No on both points. As reported, suspicion of fraud can support sharing within the safe harbour, and no link to the receiving institution’s customer is needed. Noor can ask Birchwood about the beneficiary account and share the facts she holds about the payment and the scheme. The SAR must not be sent. SARs cannot be shared and the rule makes them confidential, so Noor shares the underlying facts and leaves the report out. Because the summary is secondary, she should also check the current fact sheet and both banks’ registration. 151 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — Regulation E covers transfers initiated by someone other than the consumer without authority, and liability steps up with lateness only for later transfers the institution can show timely notice would have prevented. — Under Regulation E the institution either investigates within a short period or gives provisional credit and takes longer, and credit cards under Regulation Z carry a low fixed cap on cardholder liability for unauthorised use. — Authorised push-payment scam losses are generally outside Regulation E on a plain reading of the definition, and no general federal reimbursement rule was found. — The SAR rule is triggered by knowledge or suspicion of illegal funds, evasion or no lawful purpose, runs its clock from initial detection, and makes the SAR confidential. — Model risk guidance is nonbinding and aimed at larger banks, but a bank must still show its fraud tools work. — The voluntary information-sharing route allows facts about suspected fraud to be shared but never the SAR itself. 152

7.6.title: THE SELFIE THAT PASSED
7.6.situation: Larchmont Bank opens accounts remotely using a selfie video and a photographed identity document. Over one weekend it opens a cluster of accounts. Each has little history, receives a first payment within hours, and sends most of it onward to a small set of higher-risk payees, followed by quick withdrawals. Analyst Joel Reyes notes glitches in two selfie videos and an unusual shared device configuration. His manager says every selfie passed the vendor’s liveness check, so the accounts are legitimate.
7.6.question: How should Joel assess the cluster?
7.6.answer: Treat it as a suspected mule or synthetic-identity cluster, with deepfake use possible, and escalate. No single flag is conclusive, but the combination matches the alert: new low-history accounts, rapid payments to higher-risk payees, quick withdrawals, coordinated activity, device similarity and possible media anomalies. A vendor pass is one input and does not outweigh the pattern, and live checks can themselves be attacked. Joel should restrict the accounts under the bank’s procedures, preserve videos, device and payment records, review the vendor check, and consider a SAR with the deepfake key term where US rules apply. The pattern also fits a mule cluster (Chapter 3.3), so the investigation should not stop at whether the selfies were fake. 159 WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — The FinCEN deepfake alert gives red flags, mitigations and a dedicated SAR key term, and its red flags are not conclusive alone but gain value in combination. — The NCSC says threat actors already use AI to improve social engineering, and FS-ISAC recommends strengthening existing controls, training and a threat taxonomy. — NIST’s digital identity guidelines add fraud requirements for identity proofing, including controls against injection attacks and forged media. — The highest assurance level requires a non-exportable-key authenticator with phishing resistance, biometrics are only one factor with a non-biometric alternative, and voice comparison is prohibited. — The FinCEN alert says what deepfake fraud looks like, the NIST guidelines set the standard for proving and authenticating identity, and neither allocates loss. — Verification should rest on independent channels and call-backs to known numbers, not on a person’s judgment of a face or voice. 160

7.7.title: THE BOARD PAPER
7.7.situation: Ashgrove’s board asks Beth for a one-page view of “our exposure to scam losses” across the UK, euro-area and US businesses. Analyst Neil Fenwick produces a table with a single rule for all jurisdictions: “Customer is reimbursed within one standard period.” He lists the EU spoofing refund as an obligation about to start, citing a law-firm newsletter, and the US scam position as “covered by Regulation E”. He gives no sources. Beth sends it back.
7.7.question: What three things should Beth ask Neil to correct?
7.7.answer: First, the single rule: the UK scheme applies to authorised scams on two named systems for covered customers, and the euro-area and US positions follow other rules and clocks (Chapter 7.5). Second, the EU spoofing refund is proposed, so it is a watch item and not an obligation with a start date. Third, US authorised scams are generally outside Regulation E, so “covered by Regulation E” misstates the position and needs counsel’s review. She should also ask for the source and review date behind each row. A simple page is good, but not at the price of a false rule.

7.7.title: TARGETED OR BLANKET
7.7.situation: After the case, Colm Reeve presents two options to Beth Marlow. Option one is a mandatory confirmation call for every new-payee payment above a low value. Option two holds a payment and triggers a call only where a new payee, a high-value payment and an active phone call coincide, with the warning rewritten to name the scam. All reviewed cases shared the three signals, and the contact centre has limited outbound capacity, so Colm warns that option one would delay ordinary payments and flood it.
7.7.question: Which option fits the evidence, and what else should Beth require?
7.7.answer: Option two. The harm is concentrated where three signals meet, and Chapter 5.1 and Chapter 5.4 favour targeted rules that catch the pattern without overwhelming staff and customers. Option one adds friction and false positives for little extra protection, and a flooded contact centre would slow the very calls that matter. Beth should require a time limit for the priority queue, a measure of how many held payments were true scams, a review date, a customer-facing explanation of why a payment was held, and monitoring for fraudsters who adapt. Calls must use a number held in the bank’s records, since the scam imitates the bank. The tempting error is to pick the broader option because it feels safer. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS CHAPTER — A fraud programme starts with definitions, governance and a fraud risk assessment, with the first line owning fraud risk, the second setting the framework and the third assuring. — A map of who bears the loss for each scheme in each jurisdiction should drive priorities, and it should record the source, the review date and the status of each rule. — A large organisation in the UK has a defence if it can show reasonable procedures against fraud by employees, agents and service providers that is intended to benefit it. — Controls follow the customer journey and are layered, because no single control stops a determined attacker. — Targeted controls based on the combination of signals usually beat blanket friction, and a case review should turn one loss into a specific improvement. 163 Glossary Terms as they are used in this guide. Where a term is covered in the text, the chapter is given at the end of the entry. A glossary should send you somewhere, not stand in for the reasoning. On the day Read each question twice before looking at the options. Several are built so that the first sentence points one way and the detail points another. Where an option describes a measure that sounds sensible, ask what it assumes about the facts, and whether the facts support that assumption. A control that is right for an account takeover may be wrong for a scam, and a rule about who bears a loss in one country may not apply in the country in the question. If the facts do not support the assumption, the option is probably the distractor.
